items.title: Doña Casilda consigue quedarse en su casa de Burgos en el tiempo de descuento gracias al último decreto de vivienda
items.description: La casa de doña Casilda podría ser la casa de cualquier tía abuela de España solo que a ella un fondo de inversión la quiere echar. Le informaron de que el pasado 21 de noviembre debía abandonar el hogar en el que ha vivido 72 de sus 82 años y se libró en el último segundo por los pelos gracias al último real decreto de vivienda que se aprobó en el Congreso. La decoración evidencia el tiempo que ha pasado ahí, con muchos cristos a los que se encomienda para seguir en su hogar. Casilda Sáez, como decenas de inquilinos de esa manzana, se enfrenta a un gran especulador que ha comprado varios bloques y sobrevuela hasta que venzan los contratos de alquiler. La oferta envenenada: comprar. Comprar al inflado precio de mercado, hogares que ellos mismos han mejorado durante décadas. Muchos son ancianos solitarios de bajas pensiones. Doña Casilda suspira. Ella solo quiere morirse en su casa. El Sindicato de Vivienda de Burgos ha asistido al vecindario para, aferrándose al Real Decreto aprobado por la Diputación Permanente , prorrogar los alquileres otros dos años. Doña Casilda lo ha conseguido en el tiempo de descuento. Y aún no se le cree del todo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La España de todos: 50 hitos de la cultura y el espectáculo en medio siglo de democracia
items.description: En 1972 Manuel Vázquez Montalbán publicó un clásico de la crítica cultural: Crónica sentimental de España . En el arranque describió ese concepto: “la sentimentalidad colectiva se identifica con una serie de signos de exteriorización: las canciones, los mitos personales y anecdóticos, las modas, los gustos y la sabiduría convencional”. Explicó la mentalidad de un país en dictadura mezclando lo nuevo con lo viejo, lo culto, lo kitsch y lo pop. Ahora hemos querido mostrar la evolución de esa sentimentalidad, año a año, tras medio siglo de democracia. Seguir leyendo Coordinación: Jordi Amat y Pablo Guimón. Edición: Federico Simón. Edición Gráfica: Beatriz Palomo y Almudena Martín.

items.title: Tandoor owners threaten to stop selling roti from Dec 4 in Punjab
items.description: LAHORE: Protesting over the increasing actions of the Punjab Enforcement & Regulatory Authority (Pera) Force over using subsidised wheat flour, tandoor owners have announced that they will stop selling rotis from Dec 4 across the city. The announcement came after the Pera Force started sealing tandoor shops, having wheat flour bags procured on subsidised rates, claiming that tandoors were not authorised to procure subsidised flour. Following the action, tandoor owners had staged a protest demonstration at the DC Office a couple of days ago to demand an end to Pera actions and provide wheat flour on subsidised rates so they could sell rotis at notified rates. “All was going well and we were selling sada roti for Rs17 following the provision of a 10kg flour bag at Rs1,100. But all of a sudden, the government increased and fixed the 10kg flour bag price at Rs1,275. The Pera Force also started sealing tandoors, having flour bags purchased on subsidised rate. So far, eight tandoors have been sealed,” Mutahidda Nan Roti Association President Aftab Gill told Dawn on Friday. “While the LPG prices are already on the higher side and gas loadshedding is also ongoing, we are unable to sell roti for Rs17. Therefore, we have decided to better stop baking flatbread with effect from Dec 4,” he argued. He said the Dec 4 deadline was given just to give the government time to think and consider the demands of the association, comprising as many as 15,000 tandoors across Lahore city district. “We need 15,000 flour bags (80kg each) daily for all tandoors. If the government gives us the bags on subsidised rates, we can sell roti for Rs17, failing which, we will have no option but to stop baking flatbread,” he warned. Meanwhile, the association, through a written application to the Lahore DC, has also sought notifying the roti rate at Rs30, keeping in view the increasing rates of wheat flour. The DC was not available for comments. COMMISSIONER: Lahore Commissioner Muhammad Jahanzaib Awan on Friday visited several sites in the Walled City to review the progress of ongoing development and conservation projects, including work at Mori Gate, Taxali Gate, Sheranwala Gate and Pani Wala Talab. During the visit, the commissioner reviewed sewerage, restoration and construction work being carried out under various development schemes. Officials and engineers from the Walled City of Lahore Authority, Communication and Works Department, Nespak and project monitoring teams briefed him on the progress of the projects. Mr Awan inspected the outer drain at Mori Gate and reviewed the preservation and restoration of historic buildings. He also visited Government Victoria Girls Higher Secondary School inside Mori Gate, where he was briefed on the proposed conservation work. He also reviewed progress on the underground parking and market project at the Taxali Gate. The commissioner was further briefed on the conservation and upgradation plans for Pani Wala Talab being undertaken by the Water and Sanitation Agency (Wasa). Officials said the reservoir, established in 1883 and supported by 518 pillars, continued to serve as an important source of water supply for the city. During the visit, Mr Awan also reviewed larva surveillance activities being carried out by anti-dengue teams in the Walled City. He interacted with residents and distributed pamphlets as part of the dengue awareness campaign. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: Hope for more survivors revives after man pulled alive from rubble
items.description: KARACHI: Amid piles of rubble, the roar of heavy machinery and the constant movement of rescue workers, several people gathered at the site of the building collapse in Block 4 of Karachi Administration Housing Society, anxiously hoping that their loved ones may still be found alive beneath the debris. Rescue workers and volunteers are engaged in clearing the rubble and trying to reach those who may be trapped, while every passing moment adds to the distress and uncertainty of the affected families. Whenever the heavy machinery is halted to allow rescue workers to enter the debris and look for signs of life or recover bodies, the anxiety of relatives at the site intensifies. Some try desperately to move closer to the rubble, hoping for news of their loved ones. One family is searching for a missing brother, another for a son, while others wait anxiously for any information about their relatives. Families of those trapped in the debris express dissatisfaction with pace of search; DC says operation is continuing uninterrupted For these families, the operation is not merely a rescue effort but an ordeal in which hope and fear remain suspended between life and death. Their hopes revived when a man buried under the rubble was rescued alive on Friday, two days after the incident. Rescue 1122 spokesperson Hassanul Haseeb Khan told Dawn that after tracing the man trapped in a pocket, rescuers provided him with oxygen and, following a delicate operation lasting two to three hours, brought him out alive. “Initially, he was in trauma, but after receiving first aid, his condition is now stable. He also recorded a video message in which he told the rescue team that he, his ustad [master], and a helper were busy working when the building collapsed and fell on them, but the other two persons could not be traced,” the spokesperson added. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah expressed gratitude over the man’s survival after being trapped under the rubble for 54 hours, describing it as a “miracle”. According to a statement, the chief minister directed rescue agencies and the Karachi commissioner to expedite the ongoing rescue operation and deploy all available resources. He also praised rescue workers for their tireless efforts and directed officials to ensure that the survivor received the best possible medical treatment. 10 still trapped The Rescue 1122 spokesperson said that 10 people were still missing, as per reports submitted by their relatives at the information desk set up at the site of the collapsed building. He added that a search operation was ongoing to locate any other survivors from the debris. While families of those missing remained dissatisfied with the pace of the search operation, Deputy Commissioner East Kashif Nabi Khuhro said the rescue operation was continuing without interruption. Talking to newsmen, he denied that the pace of the rescue operation was “slow”. However, he pointed out that the collapsed building was “situated in congested, narrow streets, and it was difficult to move heavy machinery there”. Imtiaz Ali also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: Lands Ministry, Newmont set up working group to strengthen mining partnership
items.description: The Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Hon. Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah has inaugurated a six-month Joint Ghana–Newmont Working Group to address concerns relating to the fiscal, regulatory and operational environment affecting the mining company’s investments in the country. Inaugurating the group on Friday, November 27, 2026, the Minister said the initiative was aimed at creating a structured platform for dialogue, resolving areas of concern and strengthening the partnership between the Ministry and Newmont. He acknowledged the company’s contribution to Ghana’s mining industry through investment, employment, local procurement, technology transfer and revenue generation, but stressed that the Ministry remained committed to reforms that would secure greater national benefits from the country’s mineral resources. The Minister explained that the Working Group would examine Newmont’s concerns, review the relevant laws and policies, assess the cumulative impact of recent fiscal and regulatory measures and recommend practical ways to improve compliance and operational efficiency. Its priority areas include the revised royalty framework and investment competitiveness, contract mining and local participation, gold sales and pricing arrangements, foreign exchange issues, and the development of a more predictable mining investment environment. Newmont’s co-chair welcomed the initiative, describing it as an important opportunity to strengthen understanding and work through issues affecting the company’s operations and future investments in Ghana. He disclosed that the company had already committed US$4 million for 2027 to advance new projects and extensions, with further major investment decisions expected towards the end of that year. The group is expected to submit a priority issues assessment, workstream recommendations and a final report with a clear implementation roadmap identifying agreed actions, responsible institutions and timelines. The Committee includes representatives from the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, Minerals Commission, Ministry of Finance, Attorney-General’s Department, Ghana Revenue Authority and Environmental Protection Authority, alongside Newmont representatives.

items.title: Love at scale
items.description: RECENTLY, the second Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children was held in Manila. Ministers and government officials from all over the world came together to assert their commitment to protecting children, and to make concrete pledges to work towards in the next two years. Among the plenary speakers was Dr Nadine Burke Harris, a paediatrician and former surgeon general of the state of California. Her work has been dedicated to making the link between adverse childhood experiences (ACES) — including neglect, violence, poverty and abuse — and long-term impact on adults. Prolonged exposure to toxic stress has a biological response, with negative impacts on health and life potential. These can range from heart disease to obesity and substance misuse, to impact on brain development, with difficulties in learning or self-regulating. On the other hand, the experience of loving and nurturing support can have a buffering effect for children, tempering the effects of their difficult realities. Especially if support is offered early, it can transform a future. That’s why, she argued before global delegations, when it comes to child protection, “infrastructure is love at scale.” The experience of loving and nurturing support can have a buffering effect for children, tempering the effects of difficult realities. What this means is that if done right, child protection systems would represent a continuum of care. Right from prevention to recognising the signs for when an intervention is needed, to appropriate case management, response and essential follow-up. Allocating enough resources to have effective referral pathways, trained personnel and data management — that would be an act of love by those with power over budgets. In Pakistan, the scale of challenges is both vast and daunting. Where do we even start? From children visibly exposed to insecurity on the streets, to those in distant villages quietly experiencing the impacts of climate change on their households, it seems impossible to address all the structural factors behind violence. Chronic economic stress increases the risk of violence within households, as well as of child labour that sends children out without guardrails. Then there is the plethora of departments that need stitching together — health, education, social welfare, law enforcement. Each one has a role that needs to be clearly understood, so that the doctor or teacher seeing a child in suffering knows how to recognise physical and psychological injury, and who should be handling it next. The minister for human rights, speaking before the world, shared the launch of a National Action Plan and strategy for child protection. It is apt that the oversight of this strategy falls under human rights, which must be guaranteed to every child regardless of geography, ethnic or religious identity. However, what is crucial at this point is to acknowledge the need for inter-ministerial and inter-departmental cooperation, for which the MoHR can act as a conduit. The ministry of education and professional training, for instance, has a key role in ensuring that schools are both safe and enabling, and an important point of connection with children and families. It also has a key role in creating a culture of care for children, with educators beginning to disrupt the normalisation of corporal punishment and violence as a tool for discipline. In that sense, the conference was a unique opportunity to really learn from global experiences of navigating bureaucracy and politics, to get to what matters. All this being said, there are limitations to scale. Social services even in the most “developed” contexts can get it wrong, when mechanically applying standards to children or families under stress. Love at scale cannot mean that children are not seen for their individual circumstances, or are separated from families without working through challenges. If anything, love will be made up of the countless tiny acts and steps taken by the frontline workers who come into contact with vulnerable children, the conversations they are able to have, the kindness they show in response. Again, teachers can represent essential allies in a protective ecosystem. Not only do they know individuals, communities and their challenges, but can be reliable sources of support that children see every day. Within a compassionate classroom, they can create trust, joy, and hope for a positive future. The theme for World Children’s Day this year was “My day, my rights, my future.” This is not the first time we have heard words like this; perhaps that is why it is a time of great reckoning in the sphere of human rights and development, with a tragic deficit of resources and trust in the sector. However, what finally needs to be understood is that civil society alone cannot stop all the gaps, even while being able to offer the state both technical support and insights from community work. Manila was an illustration of how it is possible to make space for high-level official dialogue as well as learning from academic research, and ground-level implementation experience incorporating children’s voices. If this time we truly want love at scale, it will take all of us, working to cover the crevices that children can fall through. The writer is CEO of Cities for Children, an organisation that works to protect childhood. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: Blé : les importations devraient chuter de 44 % en 2026-2027
items.description: Portée par le rebond de la récolte nationale, la facture céréalière entame sa décrue. L’USDA prévoit 3,7 millions de tonnes d’achats de blé sur l’ensemble de la campagne, contre 6,65 millions un an plus tôt, tandis que l’orge suit la même pente et que le maïs reste l’une des principales céréales importées. Le recul des achats extérieurs de blé s’annonce comme l’un des effets les plus tangibles du retour des pluies. Dans son rapport Grain : World Markets and Trade, le département américain de l’Agriculture (USDA) table sur 3,7 millions de tonnes d’importations sur l’ensemble de la campagne 2026-2027, contre 6,65 millions la précédente, soit une baisse de 44 %. L’organisme maintient ainsi ses prévisions d’octobre. Cette contraction s’explique d’abord par la production. L’USDA estime la récolte de blé à 7,5 millions de tonnes, plus du double des 3,5 millions de 2025-2026. Dans le même temps, la consommation progresserait de 9,9 à 10,3 millions de tonnes. Récolte et importations additionnées dépassent ainsi la demande attendue, ce qui laisse de la marge pour reconstituer des réserves. Ces chiffres prolongent les annonces nationales. Le ministère de l’Agriculture avait indiqué en avril dernier que la production céréalière devrait atteindre près de 90 millions de quintaux, sur 3,9 millions d’hectares emblavés, en hausse de plus de 48 % par rapport à la campagne précédente, après sept années de sécheresse. Environ la moitié de cette récolte était attendue en blé tendre. Les estimations de l’USDA, qui ne portent que sur le blé, n’ont pas le même périmètre que ce total céréalier. Pour écouler la production locale, les pouvoirs publics ont agi sur plusieurs leviers. Le Royaume a rétabli, depuis le 1er juin 2026, une taxe de 170 % sur les importations de blé tendre et ses dérivés. L’Office national interprofessionnel des céréales et des légumineuses (ONICL) a, de son côté, fixé un objectif de stockage de 15 millions de quintaux, contre 1,61 million en 2025, avec un prix référentiel de 280 dirhams le quintal pour le blé tendre. Les minotiers se sont engagés à collecter entre 15 et 20 millions de quintaux de blé tendre national d’ici au 15 juillet. Les données d’importation confirment l’inflexion. Entre juin et septembre, les achats de blé tendre se sont limités à 59.721 tonnes, contre près de 1,49 million de tonnes un an plus tôt, soit une chute de 96 %. Sur les cinq premiers mois de la campagne, les importations de céréales et de produits dérivés ont reculé de 29 %, sous l’effet de l’effondrement du blé tendre. Le blé dur va à contre-courant : ses importations atteignent 1,06 million de tonnes à fin septembre, en hausse de 9 %. Ces volumes sont déjà comptabilisés dans les 3,7 millions de tonnes prévues par l’USDA. Le blé français n’a pas disparu pour autant des quais. Du 1er au 28 octobre, 347.825 tonnes de blé tendre ont été chargées à Rouen à destination du Royaume, alors que les professionnels français tablaient, début octobre, sur 2,5 millions de tonnes pour la campagne 2026-2027, contre 3,5 millions la précédente. L’orge connaît un mouvement comparable à celui du blé. L’USDA prévoit une récolte de 2,4 millions de tonnes, contre 950.000 tonnes la campagne passée, et des importations ramenées de 700.000 à 500.000 tonnes. Le maïs, lui, demeure l’une des principales céréales achetées à l’étranger : 3,45 millions de tonnes sont attendues, contre 3,8 millions auparavant, soit un recul d’environ 9 %. Les statistiques du début de campagne vont dans ce sens : les importations de tourteaux de soja progressent de 39 %, et la presse économique relève que le maïs prend le relais du blé tendre dans les approvisionnements. La facture reste toutefois élevée dans le sillage de la campagne précédente. Le rapport sur la compensation joint au projet de loi de finances 2027 chiffre les importations des principales céréales à 105,69 millions de quintaux en 2025-2026, contre environ 99 millions auparavant. Pour contenir le prix de la farine et du pain, l’ONICL a fixé la prime forfaitaire de novembre à 46,77 dirhams par quintal, alors que la campagne agricole 2026-2027 a été lancée le 7 novembre à Fquih Ben Salah. items.title: Messi’s defending champions Miami knocked out of MLS Cup playoffs
items.description: Columbus Crew, with an injury-time goal from Santiago Rodriguez, beat Lionel Messi’s Inter Miami 1-0 to knock the defending champions out of the first round of the MLS Cup playoffs on Friday. Rodriguez’s goal in the second minute of stoppage time gave Columbus a 2-0 triumph in the best-of-three first-round series, after their stunning 3-0 victory in game one in Florida. The defeat was a season-ending disappointment for the star-studded Miami side that features Messi, Luis Suarez, Casemiro and Rodrigo De Paul, which also came up short in the CONCACAF Champions Cup and the Leagues Cup. For Argentine superstar Messi, MLS’s top scorer in the regular season and the favorite to win an unprecedented third straight Most Valuable Player award, it was a second first-round exit in the three MLS Cup playoffs he has contested. Miami, facing a must-win game after dropping the opener at home to seventh-seeded Columbus, had chances to score on a cold, rainy night in Ohio. German Berterame had a golden opportunity six minutes from full time, but his header from point-blank range went over the crossbar. The match appeared headed for a penalty shootout with injury time ticking away. But Inter’s defense allowed Rodriguez to bring down a cross in the box from Moroccan Anass Zaroury and blast it past Canadian goalkeeper Dayne St. Clair. Miami’s early exit extends the champion’s curse in MLS. No team has retained the title since the Los Angeles Galaxy in 2012. items.title: Referendum — a non-starter?
items.description: THE idea of holding a referendum to ascertain public opinion with regard to the creation of more provinces has been floated by some ministers. The prime minister, on the other hand, remains mum on this highly divisive and potentially destabilising subject. No wonder Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari — who heads a major coalition party that also has a major stake in the current system — is vociferously decrying the government for keeping him in the dark and not taking him into confidence about the ‘reset’ or the referendum. But the visible discord among the coalition partners should not be surprising. It is in the dichotomous nature of the hybrid system. The key policies are made outside the political sphere. But the onerous task of implementation is thrown on the shoulders of politicians, often at the cost of their careers and even constituencies. The tradition of setting critical agendas — whether they are related to constitutional experiments, economic shifts, social policies, institutional restructuring, public accountability, internal security, strategic alliances, or war and peace — in secrecy and away from the public glare, is by now quite old. In many instances, even parliament has come into the picture only when the fig leaf of the law or the Constitution is needed to ‘legitimise’ a dubious plan. The ‘decision’ to hold the referendum is also par for the course. The architecture of the reset has never been elucidated. Its proponents are fully aware that a referendum can never substitute for the mandatory constitutional amendment to alter the boundaries of provinces. They also know the tainted history of referendums, which were called to validate the capture of power by dictators. And they may also not deny the fact, as rightly pointed out by BBZ, that the prevailing sociopolitical and security environment in the country is unsuitable for holding a controversial referendum, that too on such a socio-politically explosive issue. Yet, the advocates of referendum seem adamant to carry it through. Why? No one can conjecture the answer with surety because to this day the architecture of the reset has never been elucidated. All that we know is that ‘reset’ is ‘desirable’ for good governance and devolution of power to the lowest strata. But this ‘truism’ is flawed, conceptually and functionally. Conceptually, good governance and devolution being the offshoots of a broader constitutional democratic framework are antithetical to the hybrid system that is extraconstitutional. And functionally, restructuring the entire state fabric requires not only public mandate but an array of democratic tools — an elected parliament, representative governments, independent judiciary, and an apolitical (military and civilian) bureaucracy. Moreover, the increasingly arbitrary, if not authoritarian, mode of governance also makes the conversation on the imperatives of good governance and devolution rather absurd. This raises a pertinent question: are the proponents of ‘reset’ willing to do away with the hybrid system to make way for a legitimate and functional democracy, fulfilling the ‘intended’ objects of reforming governance and empowering local communities? If the hybridity is to stay, then it would be disastrous to ‘reset’ in the name of good governance or devolution, which are the attributes of a functional democracy. Even the reset on the logic of size or demographics is grossly misleading. Size and demography are only two of the many dimensions of an efficient democratic system. There are many countries where large and populated provinces are known for their excellent governance. In fact, the standards of measuring the success or failure of a political system lie in the degree of its constitutional legitimacy, electoral transparency, institutional capacity, and public administration. Therefore, the key questions probing the performance of our political system should be: is the electoral system credible? Is the public mandate respected? Are wealth and resources distributed fairly? Are public functionaries accountable? Is the justice system cheap, fair, and speedy? Is public safety and order a priority? Is the republic peaceable? And, are the citizens’ fundamental rights protected? I would advise the proponents of the ‘reset’ to consider these questions before calling for a controversial referendum that is bound to pit individuals, groups, communities, and even provinces against one another, adding more fault lines to the already much-riven ethno-cultural landscape. The people have seen enough of the ‘yes-no’ binary questions which were framed in referendums to seek personal legitimacy and institutional empowerment for military dictators, rather than reforming governance or empowering the people. Moreover, none of the referendums has earned a mark of credibility or fairness because they were rigged or state-managed. Therefore, they completely lost their utility or worth in the eyes of the people. BBZ is not too off the mark when he warns that holding the referendum is ‘near impossible’ because of the insecure environment in the country. But also, the people, particularly in Sindh, would not accept the results of a referendum, even if it is somehow carried out. Which brings us to the most critical question: what if one or the other of the provinces or a sizeable ethnic community rejected the results of the referendum? This question is crucial because there is hardly any ‘credible’ or ‘neutral’ forum — political, administrative or judicial — to resolve political disputes. Leave aside the grudges of the battered opposition, even BBZ has now cast doubts on the legitimacy of the 27th Amendment that led to the creation of the Federal Constitutional Court. And the FCC is the court of last resort in matters involving politico-constitutional disputes. Given the thick air of mistrust in public institutions, how would a ‘controversial’ referendum act as a stepping stone towards the constitutional ‘reset’? And more so when, among others, the PPP is resolutely opposing the ‘division’ of Sindh. How would the powers that be garner the requisite numbers to amend the Constitution? It would be tragic to pull off a wholesale restructuring of the state employing the carrot-and-stick method. The multiethnic state of 250 million people is too complex, conflict-ridden and even fragile to sustain yet another forced experiment. It requires meaningful dialogue, consensus-making, and democratic reforms to overhaul its political system, not a non-starter referendum or an arbitrary reset. The writer is a lawyer. shahabusto@hotmail.com Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: Giving back is success secret mother taught me — Dangote
items.description: *…why I’m teaching my daughters too Following his delivery of the Keynote address themed “The Geography of Opportunity: Why the World Needs What Africa Has,” recently at the 25th anniversary conference of Women in Management, Business, and Public Service, WIMBIZ; special guest and President/Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Ltd, Aliko Dangote, GCON sat down to a historic fireside chat with Rolake Akinkugbe Filani. The chat, anchored by the CEO, EnergyInc Advisors while also fielding questions from an audience of about 2000 women, was according to him, with the largest exclusive assembly of women he has ever addressed. Excerpts:- When your IPO closed some weeks ago, we heard that you had received a hundred and twenty applications and every single one of the 54 African countries had also applied. In your mind, Africans investing in the continent, is that one example of the geography of opportunity? Yes. What we have done with this IPO is trying to do something where, when there’s an offer in Kenya Nigerians will participate. When we did the private placement the whole idea was for us to sell 2.5 billion dollars. 1 billion was for private placement, 1.5 billion was for IPO. When we rolled out the private placement we got 3.7 billion, so we took only 2.5. What we want to do is spread this prosperity. Did this particular IPO change your view on how you mobilise capital from the African continent ? It has changed dramatically. Things are really changing very fast. Even abroad, people have a change of mind about Africa. We’ve gotten amazing demand. We’re talking about millions participating. Saudi Aramco worldwide was about 5million. We didn’t reach 10 million because of time constraints. A lot of people didn’t know how to access but the sheer trust of public enterprise that we have today in Africa, that’s why people are starting to remove their money from under their mattress to come and invest. Incredible achievement. You came from a long line of women who were in commerce, your mother, your great aunt and even your step grandmother. We want to hear if there are principles you learned by watching, by trends, by conversations, from the women in your family. From my mum it’s learning how to give back. she was always talking about giving back and she in the 80s would make sure that everyday we were feeding the poor, about 12000 people, three square meals and then we gave about 35,000 loaves of bread everyday. But right now, because there are so many in need I don’t want to announce it here, but we are looking at the possibilities of going to most of the vulnerable people to see if we can we do XYZ. We’re targeting feeding about 100m people every year. My children are ready to give. As a Muslim I am allowed to allocate one third of my wealth to charity and can actually donate to you. You don’t want when something happens to you then there will be arguments, so we actually put it in writing and got all of them to sign that in the event of my debut, one third is for the Foundation. All the good we are doing now will continue. You had a lot of naysayers when you were building the refinery and every woman here has a smaller version of that whether it be delayed contract, change in FX etc and women are used to being underestimated especially when the voices become loud and progress is invisible. During those times, what was really going through your mind? I must admit that when we were building the refinery we didn’t know what we were doing. If we knew we wouldn’t have gone near there at all. I always say that my greatest enemy, if I want to pray bad for him, I will pray that he will go and start building a refinery. Right now, that is history because we not only have one in Nigeria we have one in Namibia and possibly an additional one because we have a vision and that vision is x billion per annum but the x billion per annum which was 50 billion now has moved to 60 billion. First of all you must be trustworthy because money follows trust before profit. That your name that you have, protect it as much as you can. There will still be some few people who will try some stuff but then just be very careful, don’t let anybody frighten you. Let me give you a simple example, we have never ever gone abroad to try and raise funds but in June we went out to the market to say, we don’t have a rating and we are not going to do any guarantees. We went to what we call No Deal Road Show and at the end of it there was demand of 1.3 billion. We took 750 million. They came back to us, JP Morgan, bank of America, Merrill Lynch. We are making good money now, we went and raised another 750 in July. In August we thought, why don’t we do something that has not been done for a very long time in sub Saharan Africa, which is for a company to raise 10 years’ money. The 5 years’ money we raised, we had no rating, no collateral but you won’t believe we raised money. Our interest rate was below Federal Government rate. 10 years’ money, the demand was almost 1.5 billion but we took 750m. The sky is the limit. A lot of you should try. Don’t be scared. You say don’t be scared but it’s interesting that in order to succeed in business you have to be a bit delusional. For the women here looking for business opportunities whether local or international, how do you determine which opportunity to hold on to and which to hold back on? Whether you are a man or woman, don’t go into a business you don’t understand. You must understand that business both in and out and don’t let your own management come and be telling you. Today if you tell me, go into banking, I am not going to go into banking. You take a lot of money from the bank … It’s easy when I am borrowing the money, I have to read every single dot to make sure I do the right thing. There are some things, maybe if you look at numbers, maybe building a port, you can never ever go wrong. Port will make money. The capacity of demand is there. In 24 years by the Grace of God , we are going to be at 150 million and most of us don’t know, the population growth of Nigeria is 8.7 million babies every year. We must use every available land, we haven’t even used 10% of our arable land. People should please stop taking their money abroad no matter what. Why you see that Asia has done very well is because majority keep their money in their country at home and that money is useful to their economy. That’s why we want to bring something new. We want to start having our AGM in a stadium, not in a hall. It has to be a stadium because we have millions of shareholders. We don’t have the Asian culture of savings One in 5 people today is African. By 2050 it will be 1 in 4. Yet Africa contributes less than 3 cents of every dollar global output. When you see those stats is it a warning about what we need to do? Unfortunately we don’t plan. We need to plan ahead. Now, Let’s look at the price of food, does Europe have the land to grow their food? They don’t. Everyone in the next 24 years will turn to Africa because we have 60 percent of the world’s arable land, more than 37 percent of the minerals resources, critical minerals. The difficulty and the difference is that these people have seen us keeping our money abroad, we’re not investing here so they believe there’s a danger they don’t know. We Africans must derisk the real and also perceived risk. That is the only way other people would come and invest here. The median age in Africa is 19, in Europe it’s 40. Today if we don’t change, these GenZ s, if they get tired of us they will come and drive us away and they believe we have wasted so much time and we are not doing the right things. We have what it takes to turn around our fortunes. I can’t understand how someone that has a British passport can travel more freely in Africa than Africans. We are sort of scared of our own acceleration. Today we have 240 million Nigerians, but the president of Sao Tome when he gets to UN, has the same vote as president Tinubu. Life is not about fairness. You have to make sure that you grab your own. We must give that leadership whether people like us or they don’t. When things are good, people will come. What about the female entrepreneur just starting out and doesn’t have the balance sheet to be her own one woman system. Is that sort of model even sustainable for Africa? Of course it’s sustainable. You are just looking at what has happened in the last 20 years. You should also go back to ask where I started from. I started with just buying 4 trucks and I was very happy, in fact that was the only business I did at that time because even the 500 thousand my grandfather gave me as a loan, payable when able, I returned it after 3 months. We used to call him Baba. I said, Baba, I don’t need this money. He said, why? I said I have enough. At that time people would come and deposit their money for cement. People used to queue up for 6 months to collect cement. We used to have queue for petrol since 1972. The budget of Nigeria in 1975, you know how much it was? N30bn naira, 46 billion dollars back then. Make sure you focus on addressing exports or manufacturing. I am not saying that you shouldn’t trade but trade does not have the future and benefits. All these problems that you see today will be sorted. The future is brighter than where we are now. Vanguard News The post Giving back is success secret mother taught me — Dangote appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Loose talk
items.description: WHERE the Iran war goes, Donald Trump is known for his fantastical pronouncements. Trapped in a conflict of his own making, which he cannot find an honourable exit from, perhaps the US president expresses his frustration through these questionable remarks. Speaking to his troops recently, Mr Trump said hypothetical Iranian atomic weapons could cause a “ nuclear holocaust” , which is why Tehran’s nuclear ambitions needed to be curbed. He also termed the Iranian leadership “crazy”. Mr Trump should know that the only undeclared nuclear power in the Middle East is Israel — a state that has bombed and attacked nearly every neighbour. In fact, many far-right figures in the Zionist state, including ministers, have toyed with the idea of using an atomic bomb against Iran. Even the thought of using such weapons is abominable, but when it comes to Israel, it can literally get away with murder. Mr Trump’s recent comments amount to alarmism and creating an imaginary threat from Iran’s non-existent nuclear weapons. He himself said, after attacking Iran in June 2025, that the Islamic Republic’s nuclear facilities had been “obliterated”, while the American intelligence community is of the opinion that Tehran is not building the bomb. Therefore, such scaremongering must be avoided; irresponsible talk such as this only hardens Tehran’s attitude. If anything, the international community must work to ensure that Israel is never able to threaten any of its neighbours, or any other country, with its clandestine nuclear arsenal. Nine months after the US and Israel launched the war on Iran, a stable peace eludes the region. While there are no heavy exchanges of fire, the Strait of Hormuz effectively remains closed and Iranian ports blockaded, while Iranian strikes on pro-US Gulf sheikhdoms continue. As we have said on these pages before, this is an untenable situation for the world, and particularly for this region. The anxiety surrounding the ‘no war, no peace’ status quo must end, and give way to a peaceful solution. The period between now and when the Democrats take control of the US Congress in January is particularly dangerous, as Mr Trump — goaded by Israel and his hawkish domestic advisors — may be tempted to make a rash move against Iran before his powers are clipped. Suffice it to say, another full-blown attack would be devastating, and nearly all regional states have expressed their opposition to more war. Therefore, the US should take the military option off the table, and exclusively work to resolve the crisis through negotiations. Iran must also show flexibility to allow for a negotiated settlement. If the threats and combative rhetoric from Washington and Tel Aviv continue, the possibility of a flare-up and miscalculation is very real. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: What Pete Edochie wanted to be remembered for
items.description: By Benjamin Njoku When Vanguard encountered Pete Edochie, the Lion of Africa in his den on two different occasions, it was never just an interview.It was an audience with a king. Ebubedike sat on his throne, spoke in proverbs, laughed loudly, sipped from a glass of fresh palm wine and dropped revelations that have now become timeless. Those conversations carried the full weight of Pete Edochie and what he represented on the big screen and in real life. The first encounter was in a hotel room in Owerri, in 2015, where he displayed rare qualities that set him apart from his contemporaries: his sense of humour, his values as a father and an actor, as well as his impeccable command of the English language. The second encounter was at his Trans Ekulu, Enugu residence in 2022. During the encounter, Ebubedike was in his element. His imposing duplex dotted with images of his artistic journey, laurels and his image as the godfather of the Nigerian movie industry set the tone for the timeless conversation. When you were eventually ushered into his living room, you were bound to appreciate why Chinua Achebe preferred to call him ‘Ebubedike’ after the iconic role he played as Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of the classic novel, ‘Things Fall Apart.’ The Lion of Africa roared as he sat on his throne, “You are welcome to my home, feel comfortable.” Indeed, Pete Edochie was inseparable from his movie characters. In real life, he was a man of honour and class. When you were with him, you would not be tired of laughing. Intermittently, he would smile to encourage his guests while sharing his story passionately with them. As we recount those encounters spanning our august visit to him in Enugu in 2022, his repeated battles with rumours of his death, his reflections on Nollywood, family and mortality, now read like a final testament after his death on Wednesday, due to prolonged battle with prostate cancer. His love for classical music Beyond acting, Pete Edochie was an ardent lover of classical music and once presented a programme called ‘Music from the Masters’ while working as a broadcaster with Eastern Nigeria Broadcasting Corporation, ENBC and the Anambra State Broadcasting Service. Recalling how he developed the passion for classical music, the movie legend revealed that his wife influenced his interest in classical music. “My wife influenced me. She was very fond of classical music. When I met her she looked me in the face and said: ‘there’s something you don’t know about yourself, you are deeper than you think. You are very emotional, I see you with your friends expressing yourselves at a social gathering. But deep down, you are a very serious person’. “One day, she joined me in the preview room, where we played some classical music. At one point, when we were playing some aspects of Mozart’s songs, I got drawn into it, forcing me to go back to play it again. Before I knew what was happening, it stuck,” he told Vanguard. Edochie, however, boasted of having in his archives all the works of Mozart and George Campbell who wrote songs such as “Messiah”, “Saul”, “Solomon” among others. He confessed to placing orders for classical music from abroad, and even urged his friends travelling abroad to buy classical music for him as a gift, instead of shoes, ties and wrist watches. How he wanted to be remembered There are many things to remember Pete Edochie for. His deep baritone voice. His age-long beard. His intimidating look. His danc steps and his father-figure role in Nollywood. But beyond all of these, Ebubedike wanted to be remembered for something far simpler, and far deeper. He wanted to be remembered as a man who brought happiness and joy to many homes in Africa and beyond with his craft. Speaking with Vanguard as he celebrated his 76th birthday in 2023, Edochie opened up on his legacy, honour and fulfilment: “If people feel that my contributions toward the growth of the Nigerian movie industry have affected their lives in one way or the other, it means that posterity would award me good marks. Our industry is very challenging. While you are playing different characters in movies, you are still expected to live up to your billing as a man of honour. “People enjoy me going by their reactions to what I do. It gives me a lot of satisfaction that people think this man knows what he’s doing. If I am remembered as one who injected some life into his audiences in Nigeria and beyond, I feel accomplished,” he said. It was a simple but profound desire from a man whose career spanned more than five decades. For Edochie, acting was not just entertainment. It was a ministry. It was a service. It was a calling to heal homes with laughter, with wisdom, and with stories that mirrored real life. In his own words, all he ever wanted was to bring joy into people’s homes. And by all accounts, that is precisely what he did for more than 50 years, before bowing out of the stage. Landing role of Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’ Pete Edochie did not start his journey as an actor. He started as a broadcaster in 1967 before gaining widespread recognition through his portrayal of Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s celebrated novel, “Things Fall Apart” in the 80s. Recalling how he landed that iconic role in our 2022 interview with him, Edochie said his former colleague, the late G. C. Ugwu, recommended him for the role of Okonkwo. “He was the Zonal Director of NTA in Benin in those days. Engr Ugwu had always watched me in the broadcasting house, and the moment they decided to produce the play, the first person that came to his mind, who would play the role of Okonkwo was me”, he said. He disclosed that he had never read “Things Fall Apart” before the adaptation and his first encounter with the story was through the script. According to him, he auditioned at the University of Nigeria’s Enugu campus. In his account, the production team offered him the role after hearing him read. The performance drew attention beyond Nigeria, and the BBC team travelled to the country to interview him about it. That one role changed African television forever. It made him a household name. It made Okonkwo very popular. And it made Pete Edochie the standard by which every other African actor would be judged. Narrating the story, Edochie agreed that there was always a reflection of the Okonkwo character in most of his roles in movies. “That’s what many people said. When I started in ‘Things Fall Apart’, I was 38 years old. People still call me, “Ebubedike.” Before Chinua Achebe died, he was calling me Ebubedike. He never called me Pete, and we were very close. “Each time people visited him in America then, he would ask after me. Achebe created the character and he felt I interpreted the role excellently. He named me after Okonkwo- Ebube Dike. So, many people still see me and refer to me as an Ebubedike.” He said when the script was handed over to him, he felt it was an opportunity to read the novel since he didn’t have the privilege to do so while he was in school. “I was delighted to read the novel. Before then, I had not read it, I knew nothing about it,” Edochie stated. Ebubedike was not the only actor who auditioned for the iconic role of Okonkwo, but his talent stood him out in the crowd. According to him, “there were other actors who came for the audition held at the main auditorium of the University of Nigeria, Enugu campus. The moment I walked into the auditorium, the white woman who was invited to handle the costume and other things sighted me and screamed, ‘if this man could act, that’s the man we want for the role’. “She never met me before. I walked in and was given the script. Other people were also given the script to read, and when I read mine, they shook hands with me and said, we are good to go. They said there was no point continuing with the audition. That was how I landed the role.” Before featuring in the drama series, Edochie said he had starred in other smaller productions like William Shakespeare’s, ‘Every Man’, ‘Realm of Violence’, ‘Resurrection’ and others. But ‘Things Fall Apart’, was the production that gave him prominence. Carrying my beard for 26 years Edochie’s beard was part of his identity. He revealed how he had carried the beard for 23 years as of 2023, and he would rather go to the grave with it. “I could trim it, I wouldn’t shave my beard. I will carry it till the end of my time. I have a lot of hair on my head, and there is so much power in the hair. You read about the Bible story of Samson and Delilah. Our Lord Jesus Christ never shaved off his hair. There’s so much power in the hair,” he said, noting that his beard gave him character. “I have always played a big man in my movies. If I am not a leader of a cult, I am an Igwe or a native doctor. There must be something inspiring about you. Something that frightens people, terrifies them and intimidates them when they know that you are coming. But when you clean-shave, you lose that”, he added. Until his exit last Wednesday, Ebubedike never shaved his hair, making good his vow. As a family man Many people had described Edochie as a disciplinarian, a dedicated Christian and a good husband. He wasn’t far from those descriptions. His love for his family was incomparable. In the course of encouraging his children to stand out in life, Ebubedike bought cars for them as soon as they graduated from the university. The gesture, he explained, was to inspire them. “That was intended to be a source of inspiration for them. And they had it at the back of their minds. As they were graduating, I was buying cars for them and I don’t regret it,” he added. Edochie also spoke briefly about his marriage and his background. “My wife and I were contemporaries in broadcasting. I liked her and she liked me too. With time, it developed into a very strong affection that we thought if we didn’t give a definition to our relationship before the end of the war, there would be a strong possibility that tongues would wag and I would be accused of exploiting this young girl and disappearing at the end of the day. “I hail from a very strict paternal religious background. I am not that kind of person who would be ‘in and out’ of a woman. So, we got married and that’s it.” Death rumours For years, Pete Edochie was repeatedly declared dead on social media. In February 2026, his family dismissed another viral death rumour, with his eldest son, Leo Edochie, describing the reports as false and malicious. Speaking to Vanguard on the rumour, Edochie himself laughed off the hoaxes. “I’m alive and will die when my maker calls me home,” he said, adding that hoaxes had “killed” him about seven times since 2012. Ahead of his birthday on March 7, 2026, he pointed to family history as a source of confidence: “On the 7th of March, I will be 79. My father died at 96, so we have longevity in my family.” But he didn’t live up to his father’s age. Each time the rumour of death came, he kept going with strength to continue working. He kept shooting. He kept granting interviews. He kept showing up at movie locations. Edochie’s daughter in-law, May Edochie in her tribute after his death wrote: “For so many years, every year, someone somewhere made a false announcement of your death but you kept going with strength to continue working. This time, the news was true”. On his health challenges Although his family announced that he died after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer, the screen patriarch never named the illness publicly, speaking instead about the physical toll of ageing while continuing his schedule in Ghana and Nigeria. Eight months after his February interview, he acknowledged on camera that his mobility had declined. Visiting Ghanaian actor Emmanuel Armah at his home in Accra on Thursday, October 1, 2026, Edochie prayed with him, offered financial support, and spoke about his own symptoms. “Sitting down here, I am not very well myself. Walking is a problem for me now, but I still have hope that I will recover,” Edochie said on October 1. Despite difficulty walking, Edochie continued his Accra tour for the Pete Edochie Legacy Project on Tuesday, October 6, 2026. It was the Lion refusing to lie down. Even in pain, he was still giving. Still encouraging. Still fathering a generation. On Olu Jacobs: ‘Our mates are gone’ Edochie died ten weeks after his fellow Nollywood pioneer, Olu Jacobs died at 84 on September 16. In a recording from early May 2024, Edochie traced their bond to growing up in the northern part of the country, where Edochie schooled in Zaria and Kaduna and Jacobs spent his early childhood in Kano. Recalling their final meeting when they walked out of separate film locations onto the same road, Edochie quoted Jacobs’s words verbatim: “Olu looked at me. He had tears in his eyes. He said, ‘Our mates are gone.’ And immediately he said this, the tears came to my eyes. We just held each other like this,” Edochie said, adding that he prayed: “May the good Lord keep us so that we can represent those who are not.” He also dismissed a longstanding rumour that he had once asked Igbo film producers not to cast Jacobs, an Ogun State native, as an Igbo traditional ruler, or Igwe. “I have never disagreed with Olu for one day. No,” he said. Vanguard had dubbed the pair the twin godfathers of Nollywood. Now, both are gone within a period of time, leaving the Nigerian movie industry mourning. Tributes pour in Edochie’s demise has sent shockwaves through the film industry, with fans and members of the entertainment fraternity mourning the loss on their various social media platforms. Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy, Barr. Hannatu Musa Musawa, led the tributes session, describing him as an iroko, a national treasure, and one of the finest custodians of Nigeria’s culture, language and storytelling tradition. Musawa said,”I received with great shock and deep sadness the news of the passing of Chief Pete Edochie. This is a painful loss, not only for his family and the creative industry, but for the entire nation. An iroko has fallen. “Edochie was an outstanding actor who will not be easily replaced. He was more than an actor. He was a broadcaster, a cultural ambassador, a teacher and a father figure to generations of artists. His unforgettable interpretation of Okonkwo in ‘Things Fall Apart’ remains one of the greatest performances in African storytelling, a role that brought Chinua Achebe’s iconic character to life for the world. “He was a lover of tradition and culture, and the epitome of an African man. From his commanding roles as a traditional ruler, father and elder, he gave voice to our proverbs, our wisdom, our dignity and our identity. He carried Nigeria with pride on screens across Africa and the world.” Musawa noted that Edochie’s death comes at a particularly poignant moment, as the nation gathers in Enugu for NAFEST Enugu 2026. “That he departed in Enugu, in the heart of the land he loved and served, while Nigeria celebrates its culture, is a solemn reminder of his enduring connection to our heritage. His legacy will continue to live in our films, our language, our theatre and in the countless young creatives he inspired.” National President of the Actors Guild of Nigeria, AGN, Alhaji Abubakar Yakubu, described the late actor as “a father figure in the industry” who left his footprints in the sands of time. According to him, “the country has lost a cultural treasure, and the film industry has lost one of its most distinguished figures and enduring champions of artistic excellence. Pete Edochie was more than a gifted actor. “His passing is an immeasurable loss to Nollywood, Nigeria’s creative industry and the wider African entertainment community. He was an institution whose extraordinary talent, commanding presence, professionalism and storytelling skills helped shape Nigerian cinema and bring it international recognition. Pete Edochie was a man of the people, a detribalised Nigerian who spoke different languages. He lived a noble life, a dedicated Christian and a disciplinarian. He died when the industry needed him most. But as a thorough-bred actor, he left when the ovation was loudest,” Yakubu said. Executive Director/CEO of the National Film and Video Censors Board, NFVCB, Dr Shaibu Husseini, said a giant has taken his final bow, but his legacy remains immortal. “Today, Nollywood and the entire African film landscape have lost an iroko — a towering pillar whose commanding presence, diction, unmatched proverbs and wise sayings, and whose distinguished career in broadcasting defined an era. “From his unforgettable portrayal of Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’ to decades of unequalled performance in Nollywood movies, Edochie elevated Nigerian storytelling on the global stage and championed the cultural values the NFVCB strives to preserve,” Husseini said. Dr Ali Nuhu, Managing Director/Chief Executive of the Nigerian Film Corporation, NFC, described Pete Edochie as an institution, a custodian of African culture, a moral voice, and a towering figure. “His commanding presence, rich proverbs and uncommon mastery of the craft gave Nigeria and Africa dignity on the global screen. “From his unforgettable portrayal of Okonkwo in the television series adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s ‘Things Fall Apart’ to his countless roles as a king, father, elder and custodian of culture and tradition in several Nigerian movies, he represented an era of excellence, discipline and professionalism. His departure is a monumental loss, not only to his family and the Nollywood community, but to Nigeria, Africa and the global community of arts and culture”. Edochie became famous after the iconic role he played as Okonkwo in the NTA adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s best-selling novel, Things Fall Apart in the 80s.The role not only earned him accolades, but also launched his long, celebrated career in Nigerian cinema. Known for his deep voice, commanding delivery and rich use of proverbs, Edochie became synonymous with roles as kings, community leaders and family patriarchs. His film credits include “Igodo”, “Rituals” and “Lionheart”(2018), directed by Genevieve Nnaji. He was honoured with the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) in 2003, the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards Industry Merit Award and several lifetime achievement honours. items.title: RDC: l'armée ougandaise annonce son retrait dans l'Est, Kinshasa et Kampala tentent d'apaiser les tensions
items.description: Les relations entre Kinshasa et Kampala traversent une nouvelle zone de turbulences. L’armée ougandaise annonce le prochain retrait de ses troupes de Lubero, dans l’est de la République démocratique du Congo (RDC), tout en accusant des milices alliées au pouvoir congolais de massacrer des civils. Une annonce qui intervient après les déclarations controversées du chef d’état-major ougandais, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, sur le conflit congolais. Mais Kinshasa et Kampala tentent parallèlement de désamorcer les tensions. Les deux ministres des Affaires étrangères se sont entretenus au téléphone vendredi 27 novembre.

items.title: Algérie: le président Tebboune crée un prix des droits de l'homme, des défenseurs des libertés s'indignent
items.description: En Algérie, le chef de l’État, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a institué le « Prix du président de la République des droits de l’homme » par un décret signé le 16 novembre et publié au Journal officiel mercredi 25 novembre. Cette distinction récompensera les travaux et les initiatives qui contribuent à la protection et à la promotion des droits humains. Un prix qui suscite l’indignation de certains défenseurs des droits de l’homme, lesquels dénoncent les nombreuses atteintes aux libertés fondamentales dans le pays.

items.title: Zimbabwe: un groupe chinois signe un protocole d'accord pour l'exploitation de quatre sites aurifères
items.description: La Chine renforce sa présence dans le secteur minier au Zimbabwe. Le groupe China Railway Resources et la compagnie minière Duration Gold viennent de signer un protocole d’accord qui pourrait déboucher sur plus de 600 millions de dollars (environ 548 millions d’euros) d’investissements dans quatre projets aurifères. De quoi transformer une industrie encore largement dominée par les petits exploitants.

items.title: Soudan du Sud: l'état d'urgence levé dans quatre États à l'approche des élections générales
items.description: Au Soudan du Sud, l’état d’urgence a été levé dans quatre États du pays. La décision a été annoncée jeudi 26 novembre au soir par le chef de l’État, Salva Kiir, afin de rétablir une gouvernance normale, indique le président. Et ce alors que le pays doit tenir, le 11 février 2027, ses toutes premières élections depuis sa création il y a quinze ans. Initialement prévu le 22 décembre, le scrutin a de nouveau été reporté.

items.title: L'hypothèse d'un retour dans l'Hexagone des Français jugés en Irak pour terrorisme
items.description: Une fois jugés, pourront-ils enfin rentrer ? La question se pose pour les 47 Français qui comparaissaient depuis septembre en Irak pour appartenance à l'organisation État islamique. La France s'est toujours opposée au retour de ses ressortissants, mais aujourd'hui, le contexte pourrait avoir changé.

items.title: Uduere Killings in Delta: Six trucks of policemen, yet bullets still found targets
items.description: By Egufe Yafugborhi The sound of gunfire shattered the campaign atmosphere at Uduere, Ughelli North Local Government Area of Delta State, November 23. People who had gathered for a political rally suddenly scrambled for safety. Women ran, campaigners scattered and, in the ensuing chaos, bullets found human targets. By the time the shooting stopped, families had lost loved ones, several people critically wounded and communities plunged into mourning. Among the disturbing details was that six truckloads of policemen had reportedly been deployed to provide security. Former Deputy Senate President, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, put their number at close to 50. Yet, according to accounts from both political camps, the violence escalated despite the robust security presence. The tragedy has since generated competing accusations between the All Progressives Congress, APC, and the National Democratic Congress, NDC. Beneath the political blame game are grieving families, wounded survivors and ordinary citizens asking why a political gathering should become a death trap. A Trail Of Troubled Political Gatherings Uduere was not an isolated incident in the build-up to Delta 2027 elections. September 18, a one-million-man march organised by the NDC in the Warri-Effurun axis was disrupted by violence, leaving persons wounded. An AK-47 allegedly recovered from a suspect identified as Collins became a subject of controversy between the party and police. The NDC alleged the suspect was released the following day, a claim that formed part of its subsequent complaints about police handling of the incident. October 3, the party held a 10,000-man march against hunger in Ughelli. The following day, the Ughelli North Local Government Council, chaired by Chief Jaro Egbo, issued a notice, sealed the business premises and impounded truck belonging to Tobore Alex Agbah, who led the march. Agbah would later become one of the victims of the Uduere violence. November 7, another NDC one-million-man march in Asaba ended in violence, with one fatality recorded. The recurrence of disturbances has fuelled allegations that NDC gatherings are being targeted by political opponents allegedly linked to the ruling APC. Delta State Commissioner for Information, Charles Aniagwu, however, rejected the suggestion of a pattern. “It’s not a pattern, because when you talk about a pattern, it means that it’s continuously and then you are linking it to be able to join one to the other,” he said. He argued: “The NDC is not being attacked, there are a number of local governments where we have not had any disturbances. The APC in Delta is holding sway, the underdogs in this case are the members of the NDC who are few.” But NDC governorship candidate, Chris Iyovwaye, disagreed, recalling the September incident. “Another thug of APC was caught with an AK-47 and was handed over to the police. To our surprise, he was let off the hook the very next day,” he alleged. On the Asaba attack, he said: “Every time we are exercising our democratic rights, they’re always there to stop us.” Regarding Uduere, Iyovwaye said the party had secured police approval and was promised six truckloads of policemen. “Yet the consequence of that is that four of our men are dead and 15 seriously injured, some of them still in ICU,” he said. Two Camps, Competing Accusations The Uduere violence has produced sharply conflicting accounts from Egbo and Omo-Agege. Egbo, who hails from the community, accused Omo-Agege and his entourage of instigating the violence. He claimed two of his associates, Prince Oharisi and a man identified simply as Oche, were shot dead as Omo-Agege was concluding his campaign activities. Egbo alleged that Omo-Agege arrived after APC members had secured the town hall for a ceremony. “He came there and started abusing everybody, according to what I was told, saying I was his PA, I was his boy, and all of that,” he said. He further alleged: “On his way out, he ordered one of his boys, Efemena Umukoro, Akhima, one of the NDC key mobilisers who lost his life in the melee, to open fire on our people.” Egbo also said the community’s President-General, Cosmos Ejovwoke, was attacked and killed. “I found out that they clubbed and shot the President-General of the community,” he said. He demanded investigation by the Inspector-General of Police, declaring: “You come to my community to kill my President-General, killing my people, and you don’t even feel any remorse? We must do something about it. If we continue like this, then our democracy is in danger.” Omo-Agege, however, accused Egbo and his alleged political backers of orchestrating the attack. He listed four members of his campaign organisation as dead, including former Federal Character Commissioner, Moses Anaughe, while about 15 others sustained critical injuries. He questioned why the violence occurred despite the deployment of policemen. “We went to the campaign with full expectations, that with six trucks of policemen deployed to that venue to protect us in that event, we expected protection for everybody in that venue,” he said. “It never occurred to us that they (police) were merely coming to watch me principally executed.” He added: “There is no way you have close to 50 policemen in a venue and a minute after commencement of the attack, all of them ran away and left only you there.” Survivors’ Accounts Of Blood And Bullets One of the most harrowing accounts came from Chief Evans Ivwurie, Chairman of Omo-Agege’s campaign organisation, who was shot during the violence. Ivwurie alleged that the atmosphere became tense as the rival political gatherings proceeded, adding he personally complained to police officers about gunfire from the opposing gathering. “The Policemen told me they (APC supporters) were not shooting guns, that they were shooting knockouts (fireworks). I said but you can see them brandishing pump actions openly, shooting it,” he recounted. He alleged that violence erupted while Omo-Agege was addressing the campaign. “These APC thugs led by Egbo, the LG Chairman, started throwing stones at the direction of Omo-Agege and our people gathered there. They ended throwing the stones and all of a sudden they started shooting.” As people fled, he said, he tried to establish whether Omo-Agege was safe, alleging a man identified as Gueke, chairman of Ughelli Motor Parks, shot him in the head. “Immediately he saw me at a close range, he just shot at me, on my head. The bullet was so heavy, I fell flat to the ground without any energy,” he said. He further alleged that the gunman shot Anaughe twice in the chest. Another victim, Agbah, who had earlier been affected by the council’s action following his October rally, was shot in the neck. During a visit by Peter Obi, the NDC presidential figure, Agbah, who was receiving treatment, disclosed that five bullets remained lodged in his body. “I’ve five bullets in me. I’m happy to see you Sir. The target was to kill me. There are five bullets in me now,” he told Obi. Mothers And Communities Mourn The killings have provoked emotional reactions beyond the two political camps. Peter Obi, who visited the families of slain Anaughe and Efemena Umukoro, popularly known as Akima, alongside Omo-Agege and Iyovwaye, condemned the killings. “This is totally unexpected during these campaigns period, that people would die because they have a different view or belong to a different party from the ruling party,” he said. “We cannot kill people, harm people because we want to be political leaders.” President-General of the Urhobo Progress Union, Ese Gam, expressed concern that political rivalry was tearing the Urhobo nation apart. “Now we’re not contending with others. It’s now Urhobo against Urhobo,” he said. “If we continue to kill ourselves like this in the name of fighting for power, who are we going to lead at the end of the day?” Unanswered Security Questions The reported failure of security personnel to prevent the violence has become a major issue in the aftermath. Lawyer and activist, Austin Nyekigbe, who passed through Uduere before and after the incident, called on the IGP to order an independent investigation into the killings and the conduct of officers deployed. Human rights lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, condemned the killing of Umukoro, describing him as a courageous rights activist. “The brutal assassination of Comrade Efemena alias Comrade Akima is senseless and despicable,” he said. “The fact that this dastardly killing happened in the presence of dozens of police officers is a shameful indictment of the Nigeria Police Force.” Niger Delta Peace Coalition Coordinator, Zik Gbemre, also demanded an investigation, insisting that politicians, alleged attackers and uniformed personnel must all be held accountable where culpability is established. Meanwhile, activist Austin Aghomi criticised Governor Oborevwori for continuing his campaign activities shortly after the killings. Apparrently laying the blame on NDC and suggesting justification for the NDC killings, the governor during his campaign tour of Oghara and Koko, had said: “You can’t go for campaign and carry gun. If you carry a gun, it means you have an intention to do something. “You cannot come to my community and kill my president-general, and the community will let you go? No! You can’t do that. It’s not done anywhere.” Aghomi faulted the governor’s response, arguing that the police had a duty to prevent violence at the gathering. For the families who have to bury loved ones, political accusations cannot restore lost lives. For survivors as Ivwurie and Agbah, the battle to recover continues. The questions remain: Who tried to stop a party from campaigning? Who fired the fatal shots? Why did the police reportedly fail to stop the violence despite their deployment? And will an independent investigation establish responsibility? As Delta approaches 2027, citizens should not have to risk their lives to exercise their democratic rights. Six truckloads of policemen were reportedly deployed to Uduere. Yet the bullets still found their targets. The dead cannot speak, but their families and the survivors are demanding answers. Vanguard News The post Uduere Killings in Delta: Six trucks of policemen, yet bullets still found targets appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Government targets 2027 completion of Azumah Nelson Sports Complex
items.description: Construction work on the Azumah Nelson Sports Complex has resumed, with the government setting 2027 as the target for completing the long-delayed facility. The National Youth Authority (NYA), which is overseeing the project, says efforts are underway to accelerate construction, with the football pitch expected to be ready for use by the end of this year. Other major components, including the spectator stands, tartan tracks and pavements, are also being worked on as part of the broader development of the complex. To support the renewed construction drive, the Authority has committed GH¢5 million from its 2026 capital expenditure to the project and made provision for an additional GH¢10 million in its 2027 allocation. The Chief Executive Officer of the NYA, Osman Ayariga, said the project had encountered delays because the government inherited an existing contract with outstanding payments to the contractor. Those financial obligations, he explained, had contributed to the suspension of work on the facility. Mr Ayariga said the outstanding challenges had since been addressed sufficiently for the contractor to return to the site and resume construction. He gave an assurance that the Authority would sustain the momentum to ensure the complex was completed within the government’s 2027 target. The resumption of work is expected to advance efforts to provide the area with a modern sporting facility, with the football pitch and other planned infrastructure forming key components of the development. When completed, the complex is expected to provide facilities for sporting activities, including football and athletics.

items.title: Desperate bid to reunite with family ends in tragedy at Line of Control
items.description: MUZAFFARABAD: For Kashmi­­ris whose aspirations for self-determination remain unfulfilled, the tragedy of a divided homeland continues to take a devastating human toll. The death of 54-year-old Irfan Hassan Shah is the latest example. Shah’s body was spotted on Monday morning floating in the icy Neelum River near Keran village in Neelum Valley. Since the river forms the Line of Control (LoC), retrieving the body was a challenging operation involving rescue officials and a local army unit. An identity card issued by the Indian government identified the deceased as Irfan Hassan Shah, son of Ghulam Hassan Shah, born in April 1972. Officials initially planned to hand over his body to Indian authorities through a suspension bridge linking Chilyana in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) with Titwal across the LoC. Separated from his AJK-born wife, three sons after their deportation to Pakistan, Irfan drowned while attempting to swim across Neelum River from held Kashmir However, a photograph of the identity card posted on social media brought an unexpected revelation. Muzaffarabad-based journalist Akhtar Hussain Bukhari recognised Shah as his sister’s husband and the father of her three sons. Shah, a resident of Baramulla dist­­­­­­rict in occupied Kashmir, cros­sed over into AJK, and married Bukhari’s sister in 2002. The couple had two sons. But 2008 proved a poisoned chalice for many Kashmiris, including Shah. That year, then chief minister Omar Abdullah announced an amnesty for former Kashmiri freedom fighters living in AJK, inviting them to return to their homeland, surrender before the authorities and lead normal lives. The offer, however, proved illusory for many Kashmiris who had married in AJK. They returned across the divide with their families, only to find that the promises made to them were all hollow. While nearly all former fighters remained under strict surveillance, Indian authorities refused to recognise their wives and children, let alone grant them citizenship, according to family members. Last year, following the Pahal­gam attack, which India blamed on Pakistan, the families of former freedom fighters including their AJK-born wives and children, once again found themselves bearing the brunt of the deteriorating situation. By then, Shah had become a father for the third time. However, Indian authorities put the women and children from AJK on buses and handed them over to Pakistani authorities at the Wagha border, separating them from their husbands and fathers. Shah’s life became increasingly miserable in the absence of his family, while Indian forces stepped up pressure on his relatives. Fearing torture if he surrendered, Shah apparently decided on Monday to swim across the Neelum River from Keran to the AJK side. However, the seemingly shallow winter river proved fatal. “He believed that reporting to the Indian army camp would mean being tortured to death. Crossing the river was also fraught with danger, but he apparently considered it the lesser of the two risks,” a family member told Dawn. Meanwhile, Bukhari’s timely intervention prevented Shah’s body from being handed over to Indian authorities. After recognising the identity card on social media, he contacted officials in Athmuqam and explained that Shah’s wife and children lived in Muzaffarabad. “I was sipping tea in the press club canteen when, as part of my routine, I browsed social media and came across images of the body posted by rescue officials in Neelum Valley. I was stunned. I immediately contacted officials in Athmuqam and informed them that Shah’s wife and children were living in Muzaffarabad, requesting that his body not be handed over to Indian authorities,” Bukhari told Dawn. The body was shifted to a mortuary in Muzaffarabad on Tuesday and handed over to the family on Wednesday after completion of the formalities, including approval conveyed by his family in held Kashmir through Indian authorities. His coffin was draped in the Pakistani flag. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026
