items.title: How Tinubu fought Obasanjo to reclaim Lagos coastline – Fashola
items.description: By Juliet Umeh As the 2027 general elections draw closer, political defections, shifting alliances and questions about leadership are beginning to shape the debate over who should govern Nigeria for another four years. But for former Lagos State Governor, Mr Babatunde Fashola, one important test for anyone seeking to lead the country is the ability to build relationships, work with others and remain committed to a political team, even in difficult times. Fashola believes President Bola Tinubu has demonstrated these qualities, arguing that his ability to retain political associates and bring former opponents into his camp makes him better placed to manage Nigeria’s diversity. In a pointed challenge to opposition leaders, the former governor asked voters to examine what happened to the people who worked with other presidential contenders and why many of them were no longer in their political camps. Speaking during an interview on Arise Television, Fashola said political relationships should serve as a reference point for assessing the leadership capacity of those seeking the presidency. “Where are all the people who worked with them today? That’s a job reference question. For those who want to vote, where are all the people who worked with these people? Why is it only President Tinubu that has all those who worked with him when he was governor still with him? And they were with him for 16 years or so, out of office, when he wasn’t a president,” he said. According to him, the ability to work with people is essential for anyone entrusted with managing a country as diverse as Nigeria. “If you are going to get entrusted with managing Nigeria’s diverse family, you must be able to work in a team. And you don’t just get up and jump away when there’s a crisis in the fold,” he said. Fashola noted that Tinubu remained in the All Progressives Congress, APC, despite internal disagreements, while some political leaders had abandoned parties that helped build their political careers. He also pointed to Tinubu’s ability to bring former opponents into his political fold, describing it as evidence of his capacity to build relationships across political divides. “Not just those who worked with him before, those who opposed him are now working with him. That’s how he has built a coalition of 30 state governors from one state, from Lagos. And that is profound, whether you like him or not,” he said. Why I refused to join another party Fashola’s argument about political loyalty also reflects his own experience as Lagos governor, when he said he resisted pressure to abandon his political platform in exchange for certain benefits from the Federal Government. He recalled that during a meeting with a former President, an unnamed governor suggested that Lagos would only regain access to Lagos House, Marina, if he joined the ruling party at the time. Fashola said he rejected the condition, insisting that political conviction should not be traded for government privileges. “I said, look, Mr President, if that is the condition, keep the house. And as long as I am alive, I won’t join your party. If unfortunately I die, and they bring my body into your party, I’ll wake up,” he recalled. He said his administration also faced disagreements with the Federal Government over issues including approval for the proposed Lekki Port and access to funds belonging to Lagos State. How Tinubu fought Obasanjo over Lagos coastline Fashola also defended Tinubu’s claim that he played a major role in efforts to protect the Lagos coastline from the Atlantic Ocean, particularly around Victoria Island. He recalled that the Federal Government had spent about N4 billion pumping sand to protect the coastline, but erosion continued to threaten properties and infrastructure. According to him, Tinubu repeatedly wrote to former President Olusegun Obasanjo seeking approval for a lasting solution, but the requests were initially rejected. Fashola, who served as Tinubu’s Chief of Staff at the time, said he personally drafted several of the letters. “I drafted those letters on his instructions to President Obasanjo every time. President Obasanjo would reply, no. The last one, I think it was something like, almost like, look, get out of my life, I will find a copy of the letter. I still have it in my records,” he said. He said about seven letters were written, with Tinubu insisting that the administration should continue pressing for approval. “Nobody should take the credit away from him. I was his Chief of Staff,” Fashola said, maintaining that Tinubu deserved recognition for the initiative. Certificate controversy, foreign trips On the controversy surrounding Tinubu’s academic records, Fashola described the debate as a distraction from pressing national issues, arguing that attention should instead be focused on the cost of living, fuel prices, employment, education and security. “How does this (controversy on certificate) reduce the cost of living crisis? No, how does that reduce the cost of fuel? How does it reduce their travel time? How does it pay their children’s school fees, which NELFUND does? How does it create jobs?” he asked. He also defended the President’s foreign trips, while acknowledging that Nigerians had the right to demand explanations about public spending. “Nigerians are entitled to ask questions about their president’s utilisation of the time and resources,” he said. However, he challenged opposition parties to go beyond criticising the administration and present practical alternatives to its policies. He argued that international engagements could support investment, infrastructure development and service delivery. Funsho Williams: Fashola seeks better investigations Away from the 2027 political debate, Fashola reflected on the unresolved murder of former Lagos governorship aspirant, Funsho Williams, who was killed at his Ikoyi residence in July 2006. Following the discharge and acquittal of the six men charged over the case in 2014, Fashola expressed sympathy with the Williams family, describing the late politician as a peaceful man and an outstanding public servant. “Funsho Williams was a man of peace, a fine gentleman, an outstanding public servant. No one deserved to be treated the way he was cruelly murdered,” he said. He said the case demonstrated the need for more effective police investigations and the use of forensic tools, including DNA analysis and fingerprint evidence, to identify suspects and secure convictions. Fashola also called for the prosecution of sponsors of electoral violence, arguing that holding prominent offenders accountable could discourage others. He, however, opposed the ‘rig and die’ slogan for election riggers, insisting that punishment must follow the law and respect due process. Electricity providers owe Nigerians explanation On Nigeria’s persistent electricity challenges, the former Minister of Power said electricity providers must explain their service failures to consumers. He recalled that more than 11 million Nigerians were connected to electricity during his four years as Minister of Power, adding that his administration pursued incremental improvements towards stable and uninterrupted supply. Fashola also welcomed the decentralisation of the power sector, saying greater participation by state governments could attract investment and introduce new solutions. No plans to return to politics After years in public service, Fashola said he was rebuilding his legal practice and had no immediate plans to return to elective politics. Asked whether he would consider another political contest, he suggested that his time in public office had run its course. “I’ve run as hard as I can. So it’s time to stop running. It was a very humbling privilege to have served my country. I don’t take that for granted,” he said. items.title: Ken Ashigbey calls for mining industry excellence to become national standard
items.description: The Convenor of the Media Coalition Against Illegal Mining (MCAM), Ing. Kenneth Ashigbey, has called for excellence, professionalism, discipline and commitment to safety in Ghana’s mining industry to become standards embraced across the country’s economy. He said the mining industry’s pursuit of excellence should extend beyond winning awards and recognising outstanding performance to influencing workplace practices, business growth, community development and national productivity. Speaking at the 12th Ghana Mining Industry Awards in Accra on Friday, November 27, Ing. Ashigbey said making excellence an everyday standard could significantly transform the mining industry and the country as a whole. He urged industry players to envision a mining sector where workers returned safely to their families after every shift, businesses supplying mines expanded into competitive manufacturing, and mining communities became centres of economic opportunity. “Excellency, truly, must become our everyday standard. If excellency tonight became our everyday standard across our entire industry, and indeed our country, imagine every mine worker return home safely to their family after every shift,” he said. Ing. Ashigbey said the adoption of high standards across the mining value chain could also empower local businesses to grow beyond supplying mining companies and develop products capable of competing in markets across Africa and beyond. He stressed the importance of creating an enabling environment for businesses to expand, innovate and contribute more meaningfully to the country’s industrialisation agenda. According to him, mining communities must also benefit from the economic activities generated by the sector, with young people in such communities having access to opportunities that enable them to build prosperous futures. “Imagine every business is growing from supplying our mines to manufacturing products that competes successfully across Africa and beyond, imagine mining communities become centres for opportunity where young people can look forward to a prosperous future because mining has taken place in their communities,” he added. The MCAM Convenor further called for the values that underpin excellence in mining to be replicated across other sectors of the economy. He said discipline, innovation, professionalism and a strong safety culture were essential not only to mining operations but also to improving performance and productivity across Ghana’s industries. Ing. Ashigbey noted that the true significance of excellence lay in its ability to inspire continuous improvement, raise institutional standards and establish a culture in which quality performance became a norm rather than an occasional achievement. “Imagine the discipline, innovation, professionalism, and commitment to safety that we strive for in mining becoming the standard across every sector of our national economy. That is the real promise of excellence,” he said. He added that excellence should not be measured solely by achievements recorded in a particular year, but by the lasting impact it had on individuals, institutions and the wider society. “It is not simply about being the best in a particular year, it is about raising standards, inspiring others and creating a culture in which continuous improvement become nature,” Ing. Ashigbey said. The 12th Ghana Mining Industry Awards brought together stakeholders in the mining sector to recognise outstanding achievements, promote responsible mining practices and celebrate excellence across the industry.

items.title: Ken Ashigbey urges mining industry to translate economic contributions into lasting development
items.description: The Convenor of the Media Coalition Against Illegal Mining (MCAM), Ing. Kenneth Ashigbey, has called on Ghana’s mining industry to ensure its substantial economic contributions translate into sustainable opportunities, improved livelihoods and lasting development for mining communities. He said while the sector had demonstrated its capacity to generate significant revenue, support businesses and contribute to national development, its impact must ultimately be measured by the improvements it brings to the lives of workers, families and communities. Speaking at the 12th Ghana Mining Industry Awards in Accra on Friday, November 27, Ing. Ashigbey said the industry had made considerable progress through investment, technical expertise, innovation and responsible business practices. He cited the sector’s contribution to government revenue, local expenditure and social investment as evidence of its importance to Ghana’s economy. “As an industry, we have demonstrated what is possible, when we combine investment, technical expertise and innovation and responsible business practices,” he said. According to him, the mining sector contributed GH¢23.1 billion in taxes in 2025, representing 28 per cent of Ghana’s direct domestic tax revenue. He also highlighted the industry’s expenditure within the local economy, saying producing members of the Ghana Chamber of Mines spent approximately GH¢7.1 billion domestically, while investing GH¢88.6 million in social interventions in their host communities. Ing. Ashigbey said the figures underscored the mining industry’s contribution to national economic activity, government revenue mobilisation and community development. However, he stressed that the significance of those contributions should not be assessed solely in monetary terms, but also by the extent to which they create opportunities and improve the welfare of people affected by mining operations. “ These are definitely significant contributions, but beyond the figures, our workers, families, businesses and communities whose lives are touched by mining, our collective responsibility is to ensure that these contributions translate into sustainable opportunities and lasting development,” he said. He said the industry had a responsibility to ensure that the wealth generated from mineral resources supported long-term development, particularly in communities where mining activities take place. According to him, the benefits of mining should be reflected in improved living conditions, stronger local businesses, employment opportunities and investments that would continue to serve communities long after mining operations had ended. Ing. Ashigbey further emphasised the importance of responsible business practices in ensuring that the sector’s economic gains were accompanied by meaningful social benefits. He said the Ghana Mining Industry Awards played an important role in promoting such standards by recognising companies and individuals whose performance demonstrated excellence, innovation and responsible operations. “That is why the Ghana Mining Industry Awards truly matter,” he said. He noted that the awards were not merely a platform for celebrating achievements within the industry, but also an opportunity to encourage higher standards, inspire innovation and reinforce the sector’s commitment to responsible mining and sustainable development. The 12th Ghana Mining Industry Awards brought together stakeholders in the mining sector to celebrate outstanding performance, innovation, safety, environmental stewardship and contributions to Ghana’s mining industry.

items.title: Ndigbo ‘ve bright future despite current challenges – Bianca Ojukwu
items.description: By Steve Oko, Regional Editor, South-East Nigeria’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Bianca Ojukwu, has enthused that the future of Ndigbo is great despite their current challenges. She, however, lamented the disunity among Igbo political leaders, particularly governors in the South-East, accusing them of allowing political rivalries and personal interests to undermine the collective progress of the region. The Minister urged Ndigbo to build bridges across existing divisions and embrace unity, mutual respect and collective purpose. Mrs Ojukwu also lamented the abandonment of her late husband, the Biafran leader, Chukwuemeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu, by some political leaders who benefited from his political influence and support, accusing them of turning their backs on his legacy after attaining power. Bianca spoke at the 15th anniversary memorial of Ojukwu held at the Ojukwu Memorial Library, Owerri, Imo State, where she called for a renewed commitment to Igbo unity, peace and development. She lamented that Igbo governors had failed to demonstrate sufficient unity in addressing issues affecting the people, noting that political antagonism and mutual suspicion were weakening the region’s ability to speak with one voice. “We cannot continue to celebrate Igbo greatness while tolerating the disunity that undermines it,” she declared. The minister said Ndigbo could not demand recognition and solidarity from other ethnic groups while failing to extend the same values to one another, stressing that unity must go beyond speeches, cultural celebrations and symbolic gestures. She urged political leaders in the South-East to put aside their differences and work together for the common good, insisting that the region’s future could not be built on rivalry, personal ambition and political bitterness. Bianca expressed disappointment with some political elites who, despite benefiting from the political legacy and influence of her late husband, had abandoned him and his ideals She recalled that some politicians Ojukwu supported and campaigned for to attain political power would, upon succeeding, make removing his portrait from their offices a priority and replacing it with their own. “I know people my husband gave flag and campaigned for to gain political power, the first thing they want to do is to remove his portrait and replace it with their own,” she lamented. She said Ojukwu’s legacy should not be reduced to his military exploits, titles, speeches and political struggles, but should be reflected in his convictions, humanity and commitment to justice, dignity and the welfare of the people. Describing her late husband as a soldier, statesman, intellectual and patriarch, Bianca said his life was driven by a deep conviction that people deserved to live in dignity and without fear. Reflecting on the painful history of the Igbo, including the 1966 pogroms, displacement and civil war, she said Ojukwu’s memorial should inspire a commitment to ensuring that such tragedies never happen again. She called on traditional rulers to provide moral leadership, political leaders to rise above personal interests, and businessmen and women to invest in the homeland, while urging young people to channel their energies into innovation, enterprise and productive ventures. The minister also cautioned Igbo youths in the diaspora against the pursuit of illicit wealth, warning that criminal activities had brought disgrace to the people and landed some young people in detention rather than helping them build meaningful futures. She urged them to become worthy ambassadors of Igbo culture and contribute to creating a homeland where businesses could thrive, investors could operate confidently and families could celebrate festivities without fear. Bianca lamented the insecurity and economic difficulties in parts of the South-East, saying the region could not attract investment or encourage its people in the diaspora to return home if communities remained unsafe, businesses shut down and streets deserted. “Our land must once again become a place where our children are excited to return,” she said, stressing the need to restore confidence in the region’s business and investment climate She said Ojukwu’s ideals would only endure when they were translated into practical actions by those who inherited his legacy, noting that annual memorials alone could not adequately preserve the values of a great leader. The minister also criticised the neglect of prominent Igbo leaders and their legacies, citing the prolonged delay in completing the Zik Mausoleum. She regretted that it took former President Muhammadu Buhari to build a mausoleum for Nnamdi Azikiwe, 22 years after his death, accusing successive administrations in Anambra of failing to give the project the attention it deserved. Bianca said some leaders lived as though they were immortal but eventually faded into obscurity, unlike those whose courage, sacrifices and contributions continued to inspire generations. She thanked individuals and groups who had sustained Ojukwu’s memory through the annual memorial and particularly commended the founder of the Movement for the Actualisation of the Sovereign State of Biafra, MASSOB-BIM, Chief Ralph Uwazurike, for instituting the event. Uwazurike demands Nnamdi Kanu’s release Meanwhile, Uwazurike renewed his call for the release of detained Biafra agitator, Mazi Nnamdi Kanu, insisting that he had committed no offence deserving of his continued detention. The MASSOB founder compared Kanu’s situation with that of Yoruba agitator, Sunday Igboho, who he said had been released, arguing that the difference in their circumstances was political. “Where is Sunday Igboho? Kanu didn’t commit any offence that is bigger or more sinister than that of Igboho. The only difference is that Sunday Igboho has a brother that is presently the President of Nigeria,” Uwazurike said. He added that Kanu would have been released if Peter Obi were Nigeria’s President. Uwazurike, who advocated non-violent agitation for Biafra, cautioned youths against resorting to violence, saying many had misunderstood the principles of self-determination and allowed social media narratives to distort the struggle. He urged the younger generation to embrace peaceful advocacy, insisting that violence was incompatible with the pursuit of self-determination. “I urge the new generation of indigenous people to abide by the principles of non-violence,” he said, citing Mahatma Gandhi as his inspiration. Uwazurike said he had no regrets over the sacrifices he made in the course of the Biafra struggle, including persecution and the destruction of his residence, insisting he was prepared to make even greater sacrifices if the quest could be achieved through peaceful means. “I want to even sacrifice more if Biafra could be actualised through non-violence,” he said, warning that violence would only undermine the struggle. He lamented the absence of a unifying Igbo leader since Ojukwu’s death, expressing hope that another leader with the capacity to rally the people around a common cause would emerge. Uwazurike said Ojukwu remained a rallying point for many Igbo people despite his death, adding that the memorial was also an opportunity to promote unity and preserve his ideals. He dismissed the absence of political elites at the event, saying the memorial was primarily about the people and not politicians, whom he accused of being divided by personal interests. He urged Ndigbo to preserve unity, which he described as one of Ojukwu’s enduring legacies. The event featured cultural displays, masquerades, a march-past by delegations from states in the old Eastern Region, lectures and goodwill messages. items.title: Toxic dumping ground: Greenpeace finds UK retailers’ faulty returns at Agbogbloshie e-waste site
items.description: An investigation by Greenpeace Africa and Unearthed has revealed that dozens of electrical appliances returned to major UK high-street brands, including Tesco, Argos and Asda, have ended up at the Agbogbloshie e-waste dump in Accra, a site notorious for toxic pollution. Greenpeace is an independent global environmental organisation founded in 1971, known for investigating and exposing environmental abuse by governments and corporations through peaceful direct action and scientific research. The organisation operates in over 55 countries and refuses funding from governments, corporations or political parties to maintain its independence. Many of the items found at Agbogbloshie, including toasters, slow-cookers and kettles, were still in their boxes and labelled as faulty returns by the stores. The heaps of appliances suggest they were shipped in bulk. The findings were published on the eve of Black Friday, a period when industry research suggests one in five discounted items purchased are likely to be returned. Exporting broken electrical goods to Africa is illegal in almost every circumstance, and UK law requires used items to be tested before being sold overseas. However, the investigation found that returned goods are being sold off in bulk and shipped untested to Ghana. Faulty items returned to major retailers are likely sold through liquidation channels to “jobbers”—individuals and small businesses who buy goods by the pallet-load to extract value, including listing items on eBay or exporting them. Argos runs its own liquidation site, which recently auctioned six pallets of “small kitchen appliances RETURNS”, described as “raw customer returns that have NOT been checked or tested for faults (mainly faulty).” In Ghana, local shopkeepers told investigators that between 10 and 30 per cent of the goods they import are faulty, and many end up being dumped. The Agbogbloshie site, once ranked alongside Chernobyl as one of the most polluted places on earth, releases carcinogens through the burning of plastic. Commenting on the findings, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist, Dr Doug Parr, condemned the practice. “Customers will be appalled to learn that, instead of being repaired or recycled, these faulty returns ended up in a notorious megadump leaching toxic run-offs that poison entire communities. This isn’t the circular economy, but long-range fly-tipping, and it’s shameful,” he said. “There are laws meant to stop e-waste being dumped on low-income countries, yet this is happening anyway. Functioning and faulty items are bundled together into ‘unlucky dip’ pallets and shipped overseas, no questions asked. This is waste export in disguise, shifting the environmental and social costs of our throwaway economy onto countries like Ghana.” Dr Parr called on retail giants to take responsibility for their returns and urged the environmental watchdog to launch a full investigation. Following the findings, Tesco stated it had suspended its third-party e-waste management provider “with immediate effect” while it carries out a full audit. Argos said it “takes these findings seriously and is reviewing the information provided,” while Asda, via the British Retail Consortium, described the reports as “deeply concerning.” However, none of the retailers directly responded to questions over whether faulty electrical returns were sold off through liquidation channels instead of being processed as e-waste.

items.title: ‘Fuji Vibrations’ returns with timeless celebration of Fuji music
items.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru Lovers of Fuji music are in for a treat as Fuji Vibrations, an annual celebration returns to Lagos. The event is scheduled for Thursday, December 3, 2026, at Muri Okunola Park, Victoria Island, Lagos. Now in its sixth year, the live music platform continues its mission to preserve, promote and reimagine Fuji music, bringing together legendary performers, emerging talents and audiences from across generations. The 2026 edition, themed “Timeless”, celebrates a genre that has consistently evolved without losing its identity. From its origins in the Yoruba-speaking communities of southwestern Nigeria to its unmistakable influence on contemporary Afrobeats, Fuji has remained an enduring part of Nigeria’s expression. This year’s line-up features an exciting mix of emerging and established Fuji artistes. Representing the emerging generation are Musa Talent, Bukola OmoDaddy and Sanjay Rasheed Abefe. They will share the stage with established names including Atawewe, SK Sensation, Taye Currency, Shefiu Alao, King Saheed Osupa, Obesere and K1 De Ultimate. Since its debut in 2020, FUJI: A Opera has facilitated the introduction of the genre to new audiences through exhibitions, live performances and brand collaborations, including its international showcase at The Africa Centre in London. Its flagship concert, Fuji Vibrations, has become a fixture on Lagos’ December entertainment calendar, bringing together thousands of music lovers and some of the genre’s most celebrated performers. Speaking ahead of this year’s edition, Bobo Omotayo, Founder of FUJI: A Opera, said: “One of the most remarkable things about Fuji is how it continues to find new audiences without losing the people who have loved it for decades. The music our parents listened to is still very much part of the soundtrack of our lives today. You hear its influence everywhere, particularly in contemporary Nigerian music. That’s what “Timeless” means to us. It’s a celebration of a genre that has never stopped evolving, and the extraordinary musicians who have kept it alive.” Beyond the performances, Fuji Vibrations has become known for its vibrant celebration of Nigerian fashion and culture, particularly its annual signature aso-ebi, which has grown into a much-anticipated tradition among attendees. This year’s official colour is purple, with guests encouraged to interpret the colour through their own personal styles. The 2026 edition is supported by Supakomando, ZURI, Regal Dry Gin, whose partnerships reflect a shared commitment to celebrating Nigerian music, creativity and heritage. The event is also supported by the Lagos State Government, LASPARK, Events By Claud, AWCA, Dave Acoustics Production, Cantagali and DALA, whose contributions help bring the annual celebration to life. FUJI: A Opera also continues its longstanding collaboration with the Fuji Musicians Association of Nigeria (FUMAN), an important partner in its efforts to honour the genre’s pioneers while creating opportunities for a new generation of performers. items.title: Conquérir par le bas : à Taïwan, la Chine plane sur les élections locales
items.description: Aujourd'hui, samedi 28 novembre, 20 millions d'électeurs taïwanais voteront pour élire leurs maires, conseillers municipaux et magistrats de comté – soit environ 11 000 postes au total – lors d'élections locales, à l'occasion de scrutins qui constituent un baromètre du soutien dont bénéficie le Parti démocrate progressiste (PDP) du président Lai Ching-te. Si les questions internationales ont été reléguées au second plan durant la campagne, les résultats seront suivis de près à Pékin et à Washington. Le Kuomintang (KMT), le principal parti d'opposition au PDP, obtient habituellement de meilleurs résultats lors des élections locales que lors des scrutins nationaux. Il a remporté la majorité des exécutifs locaux lors de chaque scrutin depuis 2005, à l'exception de 2014, lorsque le PDP en avait obtenu 59 %, dans un contexte de vote sanction contre le président Ma Ying-jeou, après le mouvement des Tournesols. Le KMT devrait conserver la majorité des exécutifs locaux mais ses candidats sont en difficulté à Taipei et à New Taipei, dans le Nord du pays. À Taichung, centre industriel de l'île, l'élection désignera le successeur de Lu Shiow-yen, du KMT, qui devrait annoncer dans les prochaines semaines sa candidature à la présidentielle de 2028 face à Lai Ching-te Taiwan elections : 5 things to know about city races eyed by China and US », Nikkei Asia , 27 novembre 2026.'> 5 . Une victoire plus serrée qu’attendue, voire une défaite, dans ces grandes villes pourrait affecter les perspectives du parti en amont de la prochaine élection présidentielle. Le parti s’est rapproché de Pékin ces derniers mois, notamment dans le cadre de la visite de sa présidente, Cheng Li-wun, en Chine en avril. À l'issue de l'entretien, elle avait souligné la nécessité pour les jeunes générations de comprendre « comment, en adhérant au Consensus de 1992 et en s'opposant à l'indépendance de Taïwan, nous pouvons éviter la guerre ». Le « Consensus de 1992 » fait référence à une entente verbale conclue en 1992 entre des émissaires de Pékin et de Taipei, selon laquelle il n'existe qu'une seule Chine. La Chine, si elle n'a pas constitué une question centrale de la campagne, est néanmoins omniprésente. La semaine dernière, une candidate du Parti populaire de Taïwan (TPP) au conseil municipal de Taoyuan a été inculpée, accusée d'avoir accepté des fonds et un soutien en ligne de responsables du Parti communiste chinois pour sa campagne. Des responsables taïwanais ont également dénoncé des milliers de cas de désinformation ou d'ingérence électorale, ainsi que le harcèlement de certains candidats par les autorités chinoises Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections », The Guardian , 27 novembre 2026.'> 6 . L’article Conquérir par le bas : à Taïwan, la Chine plane sur les élections locales est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Yémen : l'ONU alerte sur le risque d’effondrement de la réponse humanitaire
items.description: Le directeur du Bureau des Nations Unies pour la coordination des affaires humanitaires, Tom Fletcher, a mis en garde contre le risque d’effondrement de la réponse humanitaire au Yémen, en raison du grave déficit de financement, appelant la communauté internationale à renforcer son soutien aux populations affectées par le conflit. Au terme d’une visite de deux jours dans le pays, achevée jeudi, le responsable onusien a souligné que près de 380.000 personnes ont été déplacées depuis août dernier, dans un contexte d’intensification des hostilités et de dégradation des conditions de vie. Lors de son déplacement sur un site accueillant des personnes déplacées à Aden, dans le sud du pays, Fletcher a rencontré des familles et des femmes déplacées et constaté les pressions exercées sur des services de base déjà fortement sollicités. Dans une déclaration publiée vendredi, le responsable onusien a appelé à un financement humanitaire accru, à la protection des civils et à un accès humanitaire sûr et durable, notamment à la ville de Taëz. Il a également appelé à la libération « immédiate et sans condition » du personnel des Nations Unies et des autres travailleurs humanitaires détenus par les Houthis. Selon l’ONU, près de 350 victimes civiles, dont 95 morts et 252 blessés, ont été recensées depuis début août. Les enfants représentent la moitié des personnes tuées. items.title: INEC tests BVAS, result portal today
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, will today run a nationwide mock accreditation and result transmission exercise in all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), about seven weeks before the 2027 general election. INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, disclosed this at the INEC and Office of the National Security Adviser, ONSA) Strategic Election Security Conference in Abuja on Thursday. He said the exercise would put the Commission’s new equipment and result systems under live conditions. “While this exercise allows INEC to stress-test our upgraded BVAS devices and verify our stricter INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV, v,lidation safeguards—which automatically block arithmetic inconsistencies and over-voting, it also serves as an essential live dry run for our security architecture,” he said. The presidential and National Assembly elections hold on 16 January 2027 across 177,299 polling units, with governorship and State Houses of Assembly elections to follow on 6 February 2027. Amupitan said the Commission had procured new accreditation machines and set a lower voter threshold for the actual election in January. “INEC will deploy over 1.41 million ad hoc personnel alongside 57,000 newly procured Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices, calibrated at a reduced threshold of 850 voters per machine,” he said. He told the gathering that the rehearsal was as much a test of coordination with security agencies as of technology. “Strategy without rehearsal is merely aspiration,” he said. The INEC chairman called on the Commission’s Resident Electoral Commissioners and the Commissioners of Police in the states to take part fully. “I urge all Resident Electoral Commissioners and Commissioners of Police to treat November 28 as a full-scale operational rehearsal: test your communication lines, evaluate rapid-response times around mock polling centres, and identify any logistical or security blind spots while there is still ample time to resolve them,” he said. INEC had earlier published the list of polling units selected for the nationwide mock accreditation exercise, naming 17,656 locations across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory FCT. The commission said the exercise is a “Mock Accreditation and Result Upload Exercise” using the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS. The list gives the state, local government area, ward, polling unit and delimitation code of each selected location. It runs alphabetically from Abia State to Zamfara State, with the FCT last. Abia has 368 entries, while Adamawa follows with 452. In the FCT, 124 polling units were selected across the six area councils. Abaji, Bwari, Gwagwalada, Kuje and Kwali have 20 each, while the Municipal Area Council has 24. The exercise will simulate the Presidential election, with polling units opening by 8:30 a.m. and accreditation running from 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. INEC said the value of the exercise lies in the faults it finds. “Its value lies in finding faults while there is still time to fix them, so a fault recorded on Saturday is the exercise doing its job,” it said. items.title: Death on the River: Some who came for rescue were more interested in stealing phones, bags, money — Survivor
items.description: By Emem Idio, Yenagoa Survivors and bereaved families of the November 20 boat tragedy in Bayelsa State have recounted their horrifying experiences, describing how passengers struggled for survival as the overloaded vessel capsized, leaving several people, including children, dead. The boat was conveying mourners from Ayama to Ukubie Community in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of the state for a burial ceremony when the tragedy occurred. One of the survivors, Mrs Lucy Africanist Olugbo, an indigene of Ijo-Gbanraun who is married in Ukubie, described the ill-fated vessel as an old boat that was unfit to carry the large number of passengers. Olugbo, who was travelling to attend the burial of her husband’s half-sister, said the passengers had initially expected to travel in a speedboat, but when none was available, a local boat was brought to convey them. She said the boat started making cracking sounds shortly after boarding, raising fears among some passengers. According to her, the vessel began tilting from one side to another, forcing passengers to shift their weight in the same direction and further destabilising it. She said water had started entering the boat while it was still moving, creating panic among the passengers. Recounting how she escaped, Olugbo said she secured a bag around her neck before pushing a heavy-set woman forward and jumping into the river. She said when she resurfaced, she saw men, women and children struggling desperately in the water. The survivor also alleged that some youths who arrived in boats, apparently to assist in the rescue operation, were more interested in collecting passengers’ phones, money, bags and other belongings than rescuing those struggling in the water. She said she personally witnessed four elderly women and a young lady die in the incident. Another survivor, Mrs Mary Silas, said she travelled with seven members of her household, including her children, younger sister and younger brother. Silas said she was particularly worried because one of her sons could not swim, prompting her to approach the boat driver and appeal to him to stop and allow some passengers to disembark. She said, “The boat was shaking and making strange sounds. Because I was travelling with my son who could not swim, I became very worried. “I approached the driver and told him that there were many children and people who could not swim on board. I told him that since we were close to the riverbank, he should stop and allow some people to come down. “He told me, ‘Okay, madam, I have heard you.’ But to my surprise, instead of stopping, he sped into the middle of the river. People were shouting, and before we knew what was happening, the boat collapsed and started sinking.” Narrating how she managed to save herself and her children, Silas said she used her swimming skills to guide her son through the water. She said the situation became more dangerous when other passengers struggling under water began dragging her, forcing her to fight to free herself. She added, “When the incident happened, I told my son to remain calm and follow my instructions so that we would not perish. I know how to swim, so I was guiding him. “Suddenly, people who were trapped and struggling under the water started dragging me. I saw a bag floating and grabbed it, then gave it to my son to hold so he could stay afloat. “I had to bite the hands of those holding me underwater before they released me. I continued swimming until I was able to reach the shore. At a point, I became exhausted, but by God’s grace, I survived. “When I got to the shore and looked back into the river, I saw many people drowning. Most of them were children between the ages of two and eight, screaming for help. The children were the biggest casualties.” Silas also accused some youths who arrived from a neighbouring community of abandoning the rescue effort to fight over and steal the belongings of victims. She said she called their attention to the people drowning but they allegedly refused to help. “By the grace of God, I survived with all my children and other members of my family,” she added. ‘I LOST SEVEN FAMILY MEMBERS’ For Dr Timi Austin, the tragedy has left a painful family loss that he said would be difficult to overcome. Austin said seven members of his family, including his wife’s two younger sisters and five children, died in the accident, while the body of one of the children was yet to be recovered. He blamed the state government and the relevant maritime authorities for what he described as a failure to enforce safety regulations on the waterways. According to him, the absence of proper monitoring, passenger manifests and emergency response arrangements contributed to the tragedy. He said, “If you are to measure how I feel, I believe there will be no proper measurement for what I am going through because I am deeply pained. I don’t know how to explain the pain, but we have to leave everything to God. However, we will take this up because it shows a failed system of government. “The Bayelsa State Government and the maritime agency have failed in their responsibilities. If there was an enforcement team monitoring the maritime sector, this kind of thing would not have happened. “I am also blaming the maritime agency because there was no manifest for the boat. Some people whose family members travelled from Delta State, Lagos, Port Harcourt and other places do not even know the whereabouts of their loved ones. “Some people may still be thinking that their family members are somewhere, without knowing whether they are alive or dead. What are the authorities going to do about such people?” Austin said his wife and daughter were initially expected to be part of the journey, but his wife changed her mind at the last minute while they were at the waterfront. He said the family had been left devastated by the loss of seven relatives. “My wife’s two younger sisters died. One had just one daughter, and both of them died, leaving only her husband. The other had four children, and she and her four children died. The last daughter is yet to be found. We have not even seen the corpse of that child. “My wife and my daughter were supposed to be part of that journey. My wife was already at the waterfront where they were loading passengers, but she changed her mind at the last minute,” he said. Asked how the family intended to recover from the loss, Austin said the pain was beyond words. “I don’t even know the process of recovery because I cannot even look at their mother’s face. Losing two daughters and grandchildren, how do we recover? It will take time, but we will take it up with the government and the maritime sector. “We are also considering taking some government agencies to court. We are consulting with people within and outside the state and the country,” he added. He further accused the state government of treating the tragedy casually, insisting that an emergency response team should have been deployed to the scene immediately after the incident. According to him, the accident happened during working hours on Friday, but the government did not send an emergency team to assess the situation until after the incident had generated public concern. ‘SEVEN OUT of EIGHT FAMILY MEMBERS’ ARE DEAD’ Another bereaved family member, Ms Diepreye Timipre, said seven of the eight members of her family who travelled for the burial died in the accident. She said the victims were her uncle’s children, comprising two women and their children, while only a little child survived after someone carried her and swam to safety. She said, “Out of the eight members of my family who embarked on that journey, seven are dead, while only a small child survived. “Somebody carried the child and swam to the shore. They were my uncle’s children, two women with their children. We were able to see and identify their corpses. We are from Ukubie Community.” ‘GIVE US A ROAD TO UKUBIE” Meanwhile, the Community Development Committee Chairman of Ukubie, Mr Reuben Kemelatei, appealed to the state and federal governments to construct a road linking the community to other parts of the state to reduce dependence on water transportation. He said the community remained devastated by the tragedy, adding that virtually every family had been affected. Kemelatei said, “Ukubie Community is in a very sad mood. From the first day of this incident until now, when we are burying the victims, we have remained in mourning. Every family is affected. There is no family that has not been touched by this tragedy. “Personally, my elder sister died at the Federal Medical Centre, Yenagoa. So you can imagine what the entire community is going through. “So far, we have recovered 35 persons and buried 29. We buried one person, a seven-year-old boy, on the first day, while 28 others are being buried today.” He appealed to the government to consider the construction of an access road to Ukubie, saying improved road connectivity would reduce the community’s dependence on boats for transportation. “My appeal to the government is to provide a road for us. We know that accidents can happen on roads too, but if we had a road to Ukubie, I believe the number of casualties in this tragedy would not have been this high. “There is a road from Oporoma to Ukubie, but there is another route from Torugbeni to Ukubie. The Torugbeni-Ukubie route will be cheaper to construct because there is no river along that route. “I am appealing to both the state and federal governments to consider the Torugbeni-Ukubie road so that our people will no longer depend entirely on water transportation,” he said. The community chairman said the state government had met with community leaders and affected families following the tragedy, but the community remained focused on mourning its dead and awaiting further directives from the authorities. items.title: Courts yet to settle if men can be prosecuted over ‘marital rape’: report
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan removed the marital rape exception from its criminal law two decades ago, but the courts have yet to settle whether a husband can be prosecuted for raping his wife, according to a new report by the South Asian Movement for Accessing Justice (SAMAJ), a coalition of 26 organisations convened by Equality Now. The report, Challenging the Marital Rape Exception in South Asia, led and authored by lawyer Sahar Bandial, reviewed the law in eight countries. It noted that the Protection of Women (Criminal Law Amendment) Act, 2006 redefined rape under Section 375 of the Pakistan Penal Code without reference to marital status, so marital rape can in principle attract the same penalty as any other rape. Yet no reported superior court judgement has confirmed this. Cases described in the media as marital rape convictions have mostly been brought under Section 377, which covers “unnatural offences”. Sherry urges action against child marriages; says one in six women in Pakistan was married as a child In August 2026, a special court in Lahore sentenced a man to ten years under Section 376 for raping his wife — a clear marital rape conviction, the report says, though only at trial level. By contrast, a 2025 Lahore High Court ruling held that forced sex within an ongoing marriage was not rape, effectively reading the exception back into the law. In November 2026, the same court dismissed a petition seeking directions for legislation on marital rape. Domestic violence laws offer only civil remedies. Regionally, the Maldives is the only country to fully criminalise marital rape on par with other rape, following a 2021 amendment. Nepal and Bhutan criminalise it with far lighter penalties. India and Sri Lanka recognise it only where spouses are separated; Bangladesh exempts husbands whose wives are over 13, and Afghanistan has no applicable law. The World Health Organisation estimates cited in the report put lifetime intimate partner violence in Pakistan at 24.8pc, below Afghanistan (50.9pc), Bangladesh (48.9pc) and India (29.9pc), though the figures do not isolate marital rape. The report urges legislators to make consent within marriage explicit in law. Child marriages Meanwhile, in a statement on the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, Senator Sherry Rehman called for stronger legal protections, effective enforcement and sustained efforts to address the social and economic factors driving child marriages. The PPP leader stressed that the practice deprived girls of their childhood, education, dignity and fundamental human rights. “One in six women in Pakistan was married as a child. Pakistan ranks sixth globally among countries with the highest number of child marriages, while more than 19 million women and girls in the country were married before the age of 18. Nearly 4.8m girls were married before the age of 15. “Globally, around 650m women and girls have been married in childhood. These are not just statistics; they represent millions of lives shaped by lost opportunities, interrupted education and diminished choices,” she said in a statement issued here. She noted that child marriages had become particularly prevalent in flood-affected areas, where families facing displacement, poverty, loss of livelihoods and insecurity increasingly viewed early marriage as a survival mechanism. “When disasters push families deeper into poverty and insecurity, girls are often the first to bear the cost. Marriage cannot be a coping mechanism for economic hardship, displacement or climate-induced vulnerability. “It further exposes girls to risks and deprives them of the opportunity to rebuild their lives through education and empowerment,” she said. Senator Rehman said the legislation had strengthened the legal framework for accountability and protection, but laws alone could not deliver justice without effective implementation, institutional commitment and public awareness. “Every girl has the right to learn, to make decisions about her own future, to grow up without fear and to live a safe and dignified life. We cannot protect our girls through legislation alone unless we confront the inequalities and economic pressures that make child marriage possible,” she said. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: PM calls for stronger Pak-Oman ties
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for further strengthening Pakistan’s bilateral cooperation with Oman, particularly in trade, investment, energy and defence. During a meeting with the Omani ambassador at the Prime Minister’s House, the prime minister highlighted the longstanding brotherly relations between Pakistan and Oman, rooted in shared history, faith and culture. According to a Prime Minister’s Office news release, PM Shehbaz stressed the importance of translating the positive momentum in bilateral relations into tangible results through increased economic engagement and institutional cooperation. The two sides also discussed recent regional and global developments. The prime minister emphasised the importance of maintaining peace and stability through dialogue and diplomacy. The Omani ambassador than­ked the prime minister for receiving him, conveyed the greetings of the Omani leadership and reaffirmed his country’s commitment to further strengthening its close relations with Pakistan. PCSIR role in exports Separately, PM Shehbaz on Fri­day directed the Pakistan Council of Scientific and Indus­trial Research to enhance its research capabilities and contribute more effectively to industrial development, export growth and the promotion of small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Chairing a meeting on matters related to the PCSIR, the prime minister said the institution could play a significant role in helping Pakistani products compete in international markets. He directed all PCSIR laboratories to obtain accreditation in accordance with international standards to facilitate internationally-recognised certification and validation of Pakistani export products. The prime minister also called for stronger cooperation between the PCSIR and the National Vocational and Technical Train­ing Commission (NAVTTC) to improve industrial and technical training opportunities for young people. He sought the report of the third-party validation conducted on the institution. The prime minister constituted a committee to review the PCSIR’s mandate, performance and future role. The committee will examine the institution’s original objectives, legal responsibilities, achievements and untapped potential, and recommend measures to improve its contribution to the national economy, industrial development and exports. The meeting was informed that the PCSIR operates 10 research laboratories and units across the country, along with seven technical training institutes, while 12 additional laboratories are nearing completion. The institution provides industries with modern technologies, research facilities and affordable technical solutions aimed at improving productivity and product quality. Officials informed the meeting that the PCSIR had provided technical training to more than 12,000 young people. Its research and development activities cover a wide range of sectors, including food, agriculture, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, textiles, leather, minerals, engineering and energy. The briefing further highlighted that PCSIR laboratories provide domestic industries and exporters with facilities for product testing, quality verification and calibration of technical instruments. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: 5.4m Ghanaians still practise open defecation
items.description: An estimated 5.4 million Ghanaians still practise open defecation, while the country spends approximately $290 million annually to address poor sanitation, the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs has disclosed. The Deputy Minister of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Rita Naa Odoley Sowah, who made this known at the 2026 National Commemoration of World Toilet Day in Bongo in the Upper East Region on November 19, 2026, described the situation as a national emergency requiring urgent and collective action. “Nationally, 5.4 million Ghanaians still practise open defecation, inasmuch as we can see that it has drastically reduced,” she said. The commemoration, held in partnership with WaterAid Ghana on the theme: “From Open Defecation to Open Opportunity through the Gender Lens”, brought together traditional authorities, government officials and development partners to renew commitments towards improving sanitation. The deputy minister said the estimated $290 million spent annually on poor sanitation could otherwise be invested in critical infrastructure such as schools, health facilities and roads. “That is money that could build classrooms, clinics and roads. So let me say plainly, this is not a small problem. It is a national emergency, and it has a woman’s face,” she stressed. She said the consequences of open defecation went beyond public health concerns, particularly affecting the safety, dignity and educational opportunities of women and girls. “Before sunrise, a girl wakes up in her home without a toilet. She must wait for darkness or walk into the bush, afraid of snakes, strangers and being seen,” she said. She explained that such experiences exposed girls to danger and sometimes prevented them from attending school, stressing that access to safe sanitation was essential to gender equality and human dignity. Bongo’s sanitation challenge The deputy minister commended the Bongo Traditional Council and the District Assembly for taking steps to address the sanitation situation through the signing of a District Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Compact and the development of a 10-year WASH Master Plan. She said the government was committed to supporting sanitation interventions through the allocation of resources to Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs), with a proportion earmarked for sanitation. “Bongo has chosen to act. Bongo signed a district WASH Compact. The Assembly produced a 10-year comprehensive WASH Master Plan,” she said. The Paramount Chief of the Bongo Traditional Area, Naba Baba Salifu Atamale Lemyaarum, said about 80 per cent of the district’s population practised open defecation, according to the 2021 Population and Housing Census. He said the situation was corroborated by the 2024 World Service Level Assessment conducted by WaterAid Ghana, which indicated that the district’s open defecation rate was more than four times the national average of approximately 18 per cent. “The irony, therefore, is that while the country is making progress in the fight against open defecation, Bongo appears to be moving in the opposite direction. This is a situation that my people and I cannot afford to take lightly,” he said. Naba Lemyaarum said the traditional council had responded to the challenge by introducing the Bongo Sanitation Challenge following the signing of the district’s WASH Compact in September 2025. Under the initiative, he said, 690 household toilets had been constructed, representing an estimated investment of GH¢2 million and providing sanitation access to approximately 3,700 people. “These figures represent much more than toilets constructed or money invested. They represent an investment in the local economy of Bongo, job creation for local artisans and expanded market opportunities for suppliers of building materials,” he stated. He further disclosed that the traditional council had established a WASH Fund to support poor and vulnerable households in constructing household toilets and improving sanitation facilities in public places. Naba Atamale said the traditional area, which had 42 communities under his supervision, was targeting the elimination of open defecation by 2030. Equality and dignity The WaterAid Ghana Country Director, Ewurabena Yany-Akufur, said sanitation was not merely an infrastructure issue but also a question of public health, equality and human dignity. She said the absence of safe toilets disproportionately affected girls, pregnant women, older persons and persons with disabilities, adding that sanitation facilities must be safe, accessible, functional and properly maintained. “A toilet is not a privilege. It is an essential service that everyone deserves,” she said. She called for stronger local government delivery systems, effective regulation and sustained behavioural change to complement investments in sanitation infrastructure. Call for collective action The Upper East Regional Minister, Donatus Akamugri Atanga, called on all 15 municipal and district assemblies to prioritise sanitation, improve access to toilet facilities and intensify public education to promote healthy sanitation practices. He said sustainable sanitation required collective commitment, behavioural change and local ownership, describing the inauguration of the Bongo WASH Fund Committee as a significant step towards mobilising resources for sanitation interventions.

items.title: AJK PM extends olive branch to protesters in Rawalakot
items.description: • Gillani says govt ready to discuss all demands within constitutional, legal framework • Urges protesters to dissociate themselves from armed groups • Speaker calls for elections to fill seven vacant assembly seats MUZAFFARABAD: Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) Prime Minister Iftikhar Gillani on Friday offered to discuss the demands of protesters in Rawalakot within the constitutional and legal framework, but urged those involved in the unrest to dissociate themselves from armed groups. Addressing a PML-N public meeting at Lal Chowk, the prime minister said the AJK government was prepared to take every possible measure, in the light of a recent resolution of the assembly, to restore peace and stability in the region. “We are ready to discuss every demand that falls within the ambit of the Constitution and law. Disa­ssociate yourselves from armed groups; dialogue can only take place within the constitutional and legal framework,” he said. Mr Gillani said some people publicly distanced themselves from armed groups but continued to provide them space, which was detrimental to efforts to restore peace. Referring to some of the protesters’ demands, the prime minister said the government was planning to establish catheterisation laboratories (cath labs) and stroke centres in different parts of AJK. The government was also pursuing road improvement projects and the Kashmir Express electric bus service, besides planning employment and self-employment opportunities for young people, he said. “Our aim is not to make a flurry of announcements but to translate plans into practical measures and deliver results,” he added. 100-day action plan Referring to the 100-day action plan, Mr Gillani said his government had drawn up a strategy extending to five years, adding that decisions concerning the state’s future and prosperity required careful planning. He said four governments had changed during the previous tenure, disrupting development activities and affecting the resolution of public problems. His administration would focus on ending political uncertainty and improving governance, he added. The prime minister said the plan covered healthcare, education, employment, tourism, transport, digital governance and urban development, with several initiatives to be implemented during the first 100 days and others continuing beyond that period. He said recruitment in government departments would be carried out thr­ough third-party agencies on merit, while interest-free loans would be offered to young people to encourage entrepreneurship and self-employment. Schola­rships at leading universities would also be provided to deserving students. Tourism promotion, public-private partnerships for government rest houses and facilities for local businesses would help generate investment and employment, he said. Digitalisation of government services through the AJK One Portal was intended to reduce bureaucratic hurdles and spare citizens repeated visits to public offices. Mr Gillani said the government would also introduce housing loans for deserving people, improve sanitation in all 10 district headquarters and undertake beautification projects in Muzaffarabad. He said the coming 100 days would provide an opportunity for people to assess the government’s performance following the Nov 18 visit to Muzaffarabad by PML-N supremo Nawaz Sharif, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz. “Building roads and public infrastructure alone is not enough; the state also needs to address its underlying problems. Society must restore moral values and mutual respect. Differences of opinion do not justify humiliating one another,” he said. Call for dialogue Earlier, Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Tariq Farooq said the government had assumed office to serve the people and promote development and public welfare. He said the Kashmir freedom movement remained the party’s fundamental objective and that it would defend Pakistan’s interests in AJK while preserving the distinct identity of Jammu and Kashmir. Referring to a recently adopted Assembly resolution, he said it reflected the common position of the people of AJK, the PML-N and all political parties represented in the legislature. Mr Farooq said the people of Poonch should regain their right to representation through elections on the seven Assembly seats that remained unfilled, thereby completing the strength of the legislature. Energy and Water Resources Minister Saqib Majeed Raja said unrest and uncertainty in AJK since 2023 had affected the region’s administrative system, economy and everyday life. He urged society to assess what it had gained and lost during the past three years, saying the support and solidarity extended to Kashmiris by the people of Pakistan were a valuable asset that should not be squandered amid political differences. He said lasting solutions to public grievances lay in dialogue, democratic processes and effective performance by elected representatives rather than protests, confrontation and vandalism. People should give their elected representatives an opportunity to resolve their problems, he said, adding that voters had the power to reject them in the next elections if they failed to meet public expectations. Several other PML-N leaders also spoke on the occasion. Published in Dawn, November 28th, 2026

items.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms
items.description: More than 260,000 people remain without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday. Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us. Conditions are now improving, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast also was affected by its own storms. Flight disruption persisted, too, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday – another busy travel day. More than 3,400 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed and nearly670cancelled on Friday. On Thanksgiving, more than 2,500 US flights were delayed and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com. One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York’s LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving. Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds. Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk. On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport. Parts of some states declared states of emergencyovernight between Thursday and Friday, including New York. Nearly 2in (5cm) of rain fell on New York City’s iconic Central Park, making it the wettest Thanksgiving on record at that site as well, according to preliminary data from the NWS. Organisers of the city’s annual Macy’s Thanksgiving parade have also pushed back the event to Saturday – marking the event’s first postponement in its 100-year history. In neighbouring New Jersey, there were multiple reports of closed roads and bridges, and images of floodwater blanketing city streets. Coastal flood warnings persisted for parts of New Jersey through the evening on Friday. “This is wild,” an Ocean City, New Jersey-based blogger said in a video posted on social media, as he waded through water splashing above his waist.

‘Poison seller’ Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
items.description: The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them. Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term. The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales. He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder. During Friday’s sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress. If Law receives the prosecution’s recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest. As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of “vulnerable people”. “What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death,” Doherty said. She also said Law’s motives were financial. “If people could pay, he sold it to them. There’s no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with,” she said. Law’s defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness.. “Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy,” Gourlay said. “Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place.” He said Law held a “misguided belief” he was helping his victims Law’s defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence. At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims. “To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I’m sorry.” The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused. Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date. Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients – who he met in online suicide forums – in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

items.title: "The World Before", un regard coréen sur les troubles de l'adolescence
items.description: Le long-métrage « The World Before » de la réalisatrice coréenne Yoon Dan-bi a été projeté, vendredi, dans le cadre de la compétition officielle du 23e Festival International du Film de Marrakech. Cette œuvre cinématographique de 115 minutes relate l’histoire de Jin, qui n’a jamais quitté l’île où elle est née. Quand Dujae, son ami d’enfance, revient pour l’enterrement de sa grand-mère et s’installe dans sa maison désormais vide, Jin trouve de petits prétextes pour lui rendre visite et peu à peu, le voir devient une habitude. Au fil de l’été, l’île qu’elle croyait connaître commence à devenir étrangère, ses visages et ses lieux familiers se transformant doucement en quelque chose de nouveau. Pour la première fois, Jin voit l’île, et elle-même, autrement. Mais l’été, comme tout le reste sur l’île, ne durera pas. Ainsi, ce long-métrage retrace les transformations silencieuses qui façonnent le regard d'une adolescente et la précipitent sur les chemins du monde adulte, lequel ne correspond pas toujours aux doux rêves que l'on peut nourrir sur les rivages d'une petite ville paisible. Possédant les caractéristiques esthétiques et stylistiques du cinéma asiatique, et plus particulièrement du cinéma coréen, ce film s'intéresse à des histoires intimes où les dimensions psychologique et sociale s'entremêlent, privilégiant une narration contemplative qui donne à voir le monde à travers le regard des personnages principaux. A l'image des grands cinéastes asiatiques, la réalisatrice Yoon Dan-bi donne voix à des émotions qui émergent d'un silence éloquent et ne s'expriment à travers les dialogues qu'avec une grande sobriété, tout en inscrivant ses personnages dans leur environnement social et naturel, qu'il s'agisse des sentiers forestiers ou des espaces maritimes. Chaque exploration du paysage permet de ce fait de pénétrer davantage dans l'intériorité des personnages, portée par une musique délicate. Sans événements spectaculaires ni rebondissements particulièrement marquants, cette œuvre ne propose pas non plus de ruptures nettes entre les différentes situations. S’agissant de la caméra, celle-ci accompagne les respirations de personnages confrontés aux troubles et aux tensions de l'adolescence, sans jamais recourir à des démonstrations dramatiques appuyées. Ce sont donc des trajectoires narratives entrelacées qui incarnent la tension entre, d'un côté, une jeune fille qui aspire à aimer et à donner de l'affection et, de l'autre, un garçon encore prisonnier des blessures de son passé et du traumatisme maternel, que ce film tente de mettre en lumière en s'appuyant sur un jeu d’acteur hors pair. Yoon Dan-bi est une réalisatrice coréenne dont les films retracent avec subtilité les transformations discrètes à l’œuvre dans les relations du quotidien. Son premier long métrage, « Moving On », a été présenté en avant-première au Festival international du film de Busan, où il a remporté quatre prix, dont le NETPAC Award. Par la suite, le film a remporté le Bright Future Award au Festival international du film de Rotterdam. Son second long métrage, « The World Before », a été présenté en avant-première en compétition Platform au Festival international du film de Toronto. Treize longs métrages, premiers ou deuxièmes films de leurs réalisateurs, participent à la compétition officielle de la 23e édition du Festival International du Film de Marrakech, qui dévoilera samedi son Étoile d'Or.
